title: fast.string
text:
Preface
fast.string is an R package for the string, date and name-matching work that record linkage and ETL pipelines spend their time on. It has three layers:
Large workloads are parallelised via Intel TBB (through RcppParallel), with PCRE2 doing the regex work and a prepared byte-oriented searcher handling fixed/literal matching. Performance depends on string length, match density, value reuse, matrix shape, and available cores. Some operations (parallel Jaro-Winkler, multi-pattern substitution in one pass) have no base R equivalent at all.

title: fast.string
text:
Why this exists
Record linkage and data-cleaning pipelines spend a surprising fraction of their wall-clock time in string operations that look trivial in isolation — trimws() on a column, a gsub() to strip punctuation, grepl() to flag a pattern — but get called over and over on multi-million-row name/address files. Individually each call is fast; in aggregate, on a 5M-row file, they add up to minutes of CPU time spent doing work a single core could be doing across eight or sixteen instead.
Four things are conspicuously not one function each in base R, despite being everywhere in this kind of pipeline:


Phonetic blocking keys (Soundex, NYSIIS, Refined Soundex, Cologne, Double Metaphone, Caverphone) — used to group probably-same names before running an expensive pairwise comparison within each group, rather than comparing every record against every other record.

Fuzzy string similarity (Jaro-Winkler, edit distance, q-gram overlap) — base R has no notion of “how similar are these two strings,” only exact (==) or pattern (grepl()) matching.

Multi-token name comparison — "Kyle John Haynes" and "John Kylie Haynes" are obviously the same person with two tokens swapped, but a plain character-by-character comparison scores that badly.

Per-element match counting — grepl() answers “is there a match”; counting how many means gregexpr() plus a vapply() that allocates a position vector per row only to take its length.

fast.string exists to make all of the above fast enough to run unblinkingly on real-sized data, and to package the boring-but-essential 80% (trimming, substitution, date parsing) so a project doesn’t need five different dependencies for five different speed problems.

title: fast.string
section: How it fits with record-linkage packages
text:
How it fits with record-linkage packages
fast.string is a toolbox of vectorised string primitives. The blocking-strategy selection, EM-based match probability estimation, and persistence of a linked dataset are handled well already by packages like RecordLinkage or reclin2 — pair fast.string with one of those for the per-string comparison work they call underneath. 12  Benchmarks at scale compares fast.string’s comparison primitives directly against the equivalent functions in RecordLinkage and stringdist at scale.

title: fast.string
text:
How this book is organised


Getting started — what fast.string is for and how it’s positioned against base R, stringi/stringr, stringdist, and RecordLinkage (1  About fast.string), then a hands-on tour of every function group (2  Quickstart).

Use cases — task-oriented recipes: cleaning and standardising text (entities, accents, abbreviation dictionaries, leading zeros, spelling variants; 3  Clean and standardise text), finding, flagging and extracting values from free text (4  Find, flag and extract), profiling and validating columns (format shapes, identifier check digits; 5  Profile and validate columns), matching, deduplicating and linking records at scale (6  Match, deduplicate and link records), and pseudonymising identifiers with keyed hashes (8  Pseudonymise identifiers).

Under the hood — the algorithms (9  Algorithms under the hood): how regex and fixed-literal matching differ, how the bit-parallel Jaro-Winkler implementation works, how the phonetic schemes trade block size against recall, and how multi-token name comparison resolves reordered tokens — followed by a full worked record-linkage pipeline (10  A worked record-linkage pipeline) that takes a messy incoming batch through profiling, parsing, deduplication, multi-key blocking, scoring, and a defensible accept/review decision.

Reference — an exhaustive per-function reference with every argument and runnable examples (11  Function reference); the heavy benchmark chapter at 3 million strings, with base, stringi, stringdist, and RecordLinkage as comparison baselines (12  Benchmarks at scale); and a troubleshooting/FAQ chapter (13  Troubleshooting & FAQ).

title: fast.string
text:
A quick taste
A whole linkage — blocking, scoring, one row per candidate pair — is one call. Two small files of people, with a surname spelled two ways, a nickname instead of a registered given name, and a date of birth whose day and month were transposed:

enrol <- data.frame(
    id      = c("E1", "E2", "E3", "E4"),
    given   = c("ROBERT", "ELIZABETH", "MOHAMMED", "LI"),
    surname = c("O'BRIEN", "SMITH-JONES", "EL-MASRI", "NGUYEN"),
    dob     = as.Date(c("1985-03-05", "1972-11-30", "1990-07-14", "1964-02-29")),
    sex     = c("M", "F", "M", "F"))

claims <- data.frame(
    id      = c("C1", "C2", "C3"),
    given   = c("BOB", "LIZ", "MOHAMED"),
    surname = c("OBRIEN", "SMITH JONES", "EL MASRI"),
    dob     = as.Date(c("1985-05-03", "1972-11-30", "1990-07-14")),
    sex     = c("M", "F", "M"))

rLink(enrol, claims,
      block   = list(exact_dob    = list(dob),
                     surname_year = list(soundex(surname),
                                         format_date(dob, "y"))),
      compare = list(sn  = jaro_winkler_tokens(surname),
                     gn  = jaro_winkler(given),
                     dob = (function(a, b) as.numeric(a == b))(dob)),
      keep    = c("id", "given", "surname", "dob"))

   pair_id index_1 index_2  pass  block_key   id_1   id_2   given_1 given_2
     <int>   <int>   <int> <int>     <char> <char> <char>    <char>  <char>
1:       1       1       1     2  O165|1985     E1     C1    ROBERT     BOB
2:       2       2       2     1 1972-11-30     E2     C2 ELIZABETH     LIZ
3:       3       3       3     1 1990-07-14     E3     C3  MOHAMMED MOHAMED
          gn   surname_1   surname_2    sn      dob_1      dob_2   dob
       <num>      <char>      <char> <num>     <Date>     <Date> <num>
1: 0.5000000     O'BRIEN      OBRIEN     1 1985-03-05 1985-05-03     0
2: 0.7777778 SMITH-JONES SMITH JONES     1 1972-11-30 1972-11-30     1
3: 0.9750000    EL-MASRI    EL MASRI     1 1990-07-14 1990-07-14     1


All three claims found their person, and the pass column says how: two on the exact date of birth, and Robert O’Brien — whose day and month had been swapped — on the second pass, a phonetic surname code plus the year alone. jaro_winkler_tokens() scores "SMITH-JONES" against "SMITH JONES" at 1, because it folds punctuation and word order inside the comparison. 6  Match, deduplicate and link records and 10  A worked record-linkage pipeline take this all the way through on data that is properly messy.
And the ordinary string work underneath it, on a million values:

n <- 1e6
nm  <- sprintf("%s %s", sample(c("John", "Mary", "Kyle", "Priya"), n, TRUE),
               sample(c("Smith", "O'Brien", "Haynes", "Nguyen"), n, TRUE))
dob <- as.Date("1950-01-01") + sample(0:25000, n, TRUE)

rbind(toupper     = system.time(toupper(nm))[1:3],
      fupper      = system.time(fupper(nm))[1:3],
      format      = system.time(format(dob, "%Y-%m-%d"))[1:3],
      format_date = system.time(format_date(dob))[1:3])

            user.self sys.self elapsed
toupper          0.49     0.00    0.48
fupper           0.05     0.00    0.05
format           5.12     0.10    5.22
format_date      0.03     0.01    0.04


format_date() is the extreme case: format() on a Date reaches strftime() once per element, and replacing that with integer calendar arithmetic is worth two orders of magnitude. Most functions here are nearer 2—10x, a few are no faster than base R at all (13  Troubleshooting & FAQ says which), and the phonetic codes and similarity scores have no base R equivalent to be compared with.

stringi/stringr are excellent, mature, and already parallel-friendly at the C level for many operations via ICU — but ICU’s regex engine and fast.string’s PCRE2 path land in similar performance territory for regex. Where fast.string pulls ahead is parallelism (stringi’s core loops are single-threaded; this package’s are TBB-parallel) and the data-linkage-specific functions stringi doesn’t have at all.
stringdist is the closest relative for the fuzzy-matching half of this package. fast.string now covers most of the same distance-metric ground (Levenshtein, OSA, unrestricted Damerau-Levenshtein, Hamming, Jaro-Winkler, Jaccard, cosine), plus a few stringdist doesn’t have at all (Dice, Tversky, token-reorder-aware comparison, the RapidFuzz scorers). The benchmark chapter measures the overlapping kernels on the current checkout. What stringdist still has that this package doesn’t is the q-gram-count distance (LCS distances are covered by lcs_seq_distance() and indel_distance()) — and it has nothing on the regex/substitution side, the text-cleaning and validation functions, or candidate-pair generation, which are the other half of fast.string.
RecordLinkage is a full record-linkage framework (blocking, EM-based classification, training), not a string-function library. Its soundex()/jarowinkler() are useful comparison points (used directly in Chapter 12) but solve a much narrower problem than the package itself.

title: 1  About fast.string
text:
1.2 Architecture
The package is a thin R layer over compiled code; almost no decision logic lives in R beyond argument validation and dispatch:





flowchart LR
    A["R wrapper\n(fgrepl, ftrimws, jaro_winkler, ...)"] --> B{Argument\nvalidation}
    B -->|fixed = TRUE| C["Prepared literal search\n(byte scan / BMH)"]
    B -->|regex| E["PCRE2, UTF-8 aware\n(base R rules emulated\nwhen perl = FALSE)"]
    B -->|trim/substr/nchar/chartr/\ndate/phonetic/jaro-winkler| F["Custom C++\n(via Rcpp)"]
    E --> G["RcppParallel\n(Intel TBB parallelFor)"]
    F --> G
    C --> G
    G --> H[Result vector]






Three design decisions explain most of the package’s behaviour:
Separate regex and fixed-literal paths, chosen automatically. PCRE2 supports the full modern regex feature set (lookaround, atomic groups, possessive quantifiers, named backreferences) that R’s default TRE engine doesn’t. The common fixed/literal case (fixed = TRUE) prepares the pattern once, then chooses memchr for one byte, memchr plus memcmp for two or three bytes, or Boyer–Moore–Horspool for longer patterns. Case-insensitive fixed matching uses a 256-entry byte-folding table instead of allocating lowercased copies of each input. Because this path interprets the pattern only as bytes, it has no regex backtracking risk. Every regular expression runs on PCRE2. With the default perl = FALSE the pattern is rewritten and compiled to follow base R’s default (TRE) rules – . matches a newline, $ only matches at the very end, backslashes are literal inside brackets, \</\> are word boundaries – while patterns that only PCRE understands (lookarounds, atomic groups, …) get perl = TRUE semantics. Text is matched by UTF-8 character unless useBytes = TRUE. See Chapter 9 for the details.
Parallelism via Intel TBB, not parallel/future. Forking R processes (parallel::mclapply) or spinning up a cluster (future) carries fixed overhead per call — serialising data to workers, process startup, gathering results back — that swamps the actual work for anything shorter than seconds. RcppParallel’s parallelFor instead splits one C++-level loop across a TBB thread pool within a single R call, with no serialisation step and microsecond-scale dispatch overhead. Every parallel function in this package applies a size threshold before bothering to parallelise at all (typically n >= 1000 for vectors, n*m >= 10000 for matrix operations) — below that, the thread-pool dispatch overhead would exceed the time saved, so the package just runs the loop on the calling thread.
Thread-local scratch buffers, not per-call allocation. The performance-sensitive C++ (the bit-parallel Jaro similarity, the token alignment in jaro_winkler_tokens()) reuses thread_local buffers across rows within a worker thread instead of allocating fresh memory for every string pair. The buffers grow to a high-water mark and then stop reallocating, so the steady-state cost of comparing the one-millionth pair is the same as the thousandth.

title: 1  About fast.string
text:
1.3 Who this is for
If you’re doing record linkage, deduplication, ETL, or any other pipeline that processes name/address/free-text columns with hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of rows, and you’ve profiled your pipeline and found string operations are a meaningful fraction of the runtime, this package is squarely aimed at you.
If your data is a few thousand rows, or your bottleneck is somewhere else entirely (I/O, a join, a model fit), the speedups here won’t be the thing that matters, and the simpler base R/stringi call is the right choice — fewer dependencies, identical behaviour, and the performance difference won’t be visible at that scale. Chapter 12 shows this explicitly: at small n, the parallel-dispatch overhead can make fast.string functions slower than their base R/stringi equivalents.

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
2.1 Installation
This compiles C++ source on install, so you need a working toolchain: Rtools on Windows, Xcode command-line tools on macOS, or build-essential + libpcre2-dev on Linux. See Chapter 13 if the install fails.
library(fast.string)
Loading the package prints a one-time startup banner listing every exported function; suppress it with options(fast.string.verbose = FALSE) set before library(), or with suppressPackageStartupMessages().
The rest of this chapter is a guided tour through every function group, using small inputs so it renders fast — Chapter 12 is where the same functions get pushed to 3 million rows.

title: 2  Quickstart
text: remotes::install_github("KyleHaynes/fast.string")

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
2.2 Matching & substitution
fgrepl(), fgrep(), fsub(), and fgsub() are argument-compatible with base::grepl()/grep()/sub()/gsub() — same defaults, same NA handling — just parallelised.

x <- c("invoice-2024-001", "invoice-2024-002", "credit-note-001", NA)

fgrepl("^invoice", x)

[1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE    NA

fgrep("^invoice", x, value = TRUE)

[1] "invoice-2024-001" "invoice-2024-002"

fsub("-([0-9]+)$", "_\\1", x)

[1] "invoice-2024_001" "invoice-2024_002" "credit-note_001"  NA                

fgsub("[0-9]", "#", x)

[1] "invoice-####-###" "invoice-####-###" "credit-note-###"  NA                


fcount() counts non-overlapping matches per element — the counting counterpart to fgrepl(), replacing the vapply(gregexpr(...), length, ...) idiom, which allocates a vector of match positions per row only to take its length.

fcount("[0-9]", x)

[1]  7  7  3 NA

fcount("-", x, fixed = TRUE)

[1]  2  2  2 NA

# Column-level quality rules in one call each
names_in <- c("JOHN O'BRIEN", "UNKNOWN 00000000", "Kyle John Haynes")
fcount("[0-9]", names_in)          # digits in a name field: placeholder rows

[1] 0 8 0

fcount(" +", names_in) + 1L        # token count

[1] 2 2 3


gsub_all() has no base R equivalent: it applies several patterns in one pass, either sequentially (chained, like calling gsub() repeatedly) or as a single combined left-to-right scan where the first matching pattern at each position wins.

patterns <- c("Mr\\.", "Mrs\\.", "Dr\\.")
repls    <- c("Mister", "Missus", "Doctor")
gsub_all(patterns, repls, c("Mr. Smith", "Dr. Jones"), fixed = FALSE)

[1] "Mister Smith" "Doctor Jones"

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
2.3 String utilities
ftrimws(), fsubstr(), fnchar(), and fchartr() mirror their base equivalents exactly, including names(x) preservation.

messy <- c("  John Smith  ", "\tMary Jones\n", NA)
ftrimws(messy)

[1] "John Smith" "Mary Jones" NA          

records <- c("NSWREC123456789", "VICPOL987654321")
fsubstr(records, 1, 3)   # state code

[1] "NSW" "VIC"

fsubstr(records, 4, 6)   # category code

[1] "REC" "POL"

fnchar(c("café", NA, ""), type = "chars")

[1]  4 NA  0

fchartr("'-", "  ", c("O'Brien", "Smith-Jones"))

[1] "O Brien"     "Smith Jones"

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
2.4 Text cleaning and extraction
Beyond the base equivalents, the cleaning functions handle what base R has no direct answer for: HTML entities, every kind of Unicode whitespace, accents, whole-word dictionaries and lost leading zeros (Chapter 3 has the full recipes).

html_unescape("Fish & Chips – open")

[1] "Fish & Chips – open"

fsquish("  12   Smith\tSt  ")

[1] "12 Smith St"

ascii_fold("Fran\u00e7ois M\u00fcller")

[1] "Francois Muller"

freplace_tokens("12 SMITH ST", c("ST", "RD"), c("STREET", "ROAD"))

[1] "12 SMITH STREET"

fpad(c("800", "4000"), 4, pad = "0")

[1] "0800" "4000"

url_decode("q=meat+pie%21", plus = TRUE)

[1] "q=meat pie!"


Extraction pulls structured values out of free text: regex matches and capture groups, one field of delimited text, any of thousands of literal terms in one pass, approximate matches, and numbers (Chapter 4).

addr <- c("12 Smith St, Brisbane QLD 4000", "PO Box 99, Hobart TAS 7001")
fextract("([0-9]{4})$", addr, group = 1)

[1] "4000" "7001"

fsplit_field("SMITH, John", ",", 1, fixed = TRUE)

[1] "SMITH"

fgrepl_any(c("aspirin", "warfarin"), c("started warfarin", "no meds"))

[1]  TRUE FALSE

fagrepl("paracetamol", "paracetemol 1g", max.distance = 1)

[1] TRUE

fparse_number(c("$1,234.50", "-$45", "approx. 3,000 kg"))

[1] 1234.5  -45.0 3000.0

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
2.5 Profiling, validation and hashing
string_shape() reduces values to their format, valid_id() checks identifier check digits, and fhash() computes digests and keyed pseudonyms (Chapter 5, Chapter 8).

string_shape(c("0412 345 678", "(07) 3123 4567", "QLD 4000"))

[1] "9999 999 999"   "(99) 9999 9999" "AAA 9999"      

valid_id(c("51 824 753 556", "51 824 753 557"), "abn")

[1]  TRUE FALSE

fhash("123456782", key = "secret")

[1] "73e89fd22fe7409a215ceb7a71b1eee7c44f09b6f14cedfb7a3c6a4273236182"

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
2.6 Dates
format_date()/fas.Date() trade base::as.Date()’s locale-aware, multi-format flexibility for speed on one fixed format at a time. date_parts() decomposes a Date vector into year/month/day columns in a single pass — useful for building blocking keys.

dates <- as.Date(c("2024-06-18", "1999-12-31", NA))
format_date(dates, "compact")

[1] "20240618" "19991231" NA        

date_parts(dates)

  year month day
1 2024     6  18
2 1999    12  31
3   NA    NA  NA

fas.Date(c("18/06/2024", "31/12/1999"), "dmy")

[1] "2024-06-18" "1999-12-31"


fas.POSIXct() and format_datetime() are the timestamp equivalents, covering four fixed shapes (iso, rfc3339, compact, iso_offset). Everything is handled as UTC seconds since the epoch — no timezone-database lookup — and "iso_offset" writes one fixed numeric offset rather than a real timezone (no daylight-saving rules).

stamps <- fas.POSIXct(c("2024-06-18 09:15:00", "2024-06-18 23:59:59", "not a time"))
stamps

[1] "2024-06-18 09:15:00 UTC" "2024-06-18 23:59:59 UTC" NA                       

format_datetime(stamps, "rfc3339")

[1] "2024-06-18T09:15:00Z" "2024-06-18T23:59:59Z" NA                    

format_datetime(stamps, "compact")

[1] "20240618091500" "20240618235959" NA              

format_datetime(stamps, "iso_offset", offset = "+10:00")

[1] "2024-06-18T19:15:00+10:00" "2024-06-19T09:59:59+10:00" NA                         


Both parsers validate the whole calendar – month lengths and leap years included – and return NA for an impossible date:

fas.Date("29/02/2023", "dmy")       # NA -- 2023 is not a leap year

[1] NA

fas.POSIXct("2023-02-29 08:00:00")  # NA

[1] NA

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
2.7 Phonetic blocking keys
soundex(), nysiis(), refined_soundex(), cologne(), double_metaphone(), and caverphone() have no base R equivalent. They’re typically used to group records that sound alike before running a more expensive pairwise comparison only within each group, rather than comparing every record against every other record. Different rulesets group different near-miss spellings together, so trying more than one can catch matches a single phonetic key misses.

names_x <- c("Robert", "Rupert", "Ashcraft", "Ashcroft", "Smith", "Smyth")
data.frame(
    name       = names_x,
    soundex    = soundex(names_x),
    nysiis     = nysiis(names_x),
    refined    = refined_soundex(names_x),
    caverphone = caverphone(names_x)
)

      name soundex nysiis   refined caverphone
1   Robert    R163  RABAD   R901096 RPT1111111
2   Rupert    R163  RAPAD   R901096 RPT1111111
3 Ashcraft    A261 ASCRAF A03039026 ASKRFT1111
4 Ashcroft    A261 ASCRAF A03039026 ASKRFT1111
5    Smith    S530   SNAT    S38060 SMT1111111
6    Smyth    S530   SNYT    S38060 SMT1111111

double_metaphone(c("Smith", "Schmidt", "Catherine", "Kathryn"))

  primary secondary
1     SM0       XMT
2     XMT       SMT
3    K0RN      KTRN
4    K0RN      KTRN


"Ashcraft"/"Ashcroft" sharing a Soundex code (A261) despite differing spelling is the textbook example of why Soundex exists — and a known point of disagreement between implementations of Soundex, covered in Chapter 9.
double_metaphone() returns two codes per word — primary and secondary — because some spellings have more than one plausible pronunciation (a C that could be a hard K or a soft S sound, for instance); two names are usually considered a phonetic match if any of one side’s codes matches any of the other’s. "Catherine" and "Kathryn" sharing the code K0RN despite no letters lining up is the kind of match Soundex/NYSIIS — designed around English/American surnames — typically miss.
The two newer schemes sit at opposite ends of the precision/recall trade-off. refined_soundex() encodes vowels instead of discarding them, so it produces a longer, more discriminating code — smaller blocks, fewer false candidates. cologne() targets German pronunciation and folds umlauts to their base vowels, so spelling variants that ASCII-only schemes split are grouped together:

german <- c("Müller", "Mueller", "Miller", "Meier", "Meyer", "Schmidt", "Schmitt")
data.frame(
    name    = german,
    soundex = soundex(german),
    refined = refined_soundex(german),
    cologne = cologne(german)
)

     name soundex refined cologne
1  Müller    M460  M80709     657
2 Mueller    M460  M80709     657
3  Miller    M460  M80709     657
4   Meier    M600    M809      67
5   Meyer    M600    M809      67
6 Schmidt    S530  S30806     862
7 Schmitt    S530  S30806     862


refined_soundex() splits "Müller" off from "Mueller"/"Miller", because the umlaut isn’t an ASCII vowel it can encode; cologne() folds it and puts all three in one block. Neither is “right” — they’re different recall/precision settings, and Chapter 10 uses both at once and takes the union of the candidate blocks.

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
2.8 Fuzzy string similarity
Three functions, three shapes of comparison:


jaro_winkler(a, b) — pairwise, equal-length vectors. a[i] vs. b[i] for every i.

jaro_winkler_matrix(a, b) — all-pairs. Every element of a against every element of b, returned as an n × m matrix.

jaro_winkler_tokens(a, b) — pairwise like the first, but tolerant of token reordering and punctuation/spacing differences within a token.


jaro_winkler(c("SMITH", "DWAYNE"), c("SMYTH", "DUANE"))

[1] 0.8933333 0.8400000

candidates_a <- c("John Smith", "Mary Jones")
candidates_b <- c("Jon Smith", "Mary-Anne Jones", "Someone Else")
jaro_winkler_matrix(candidates_a, candidates_b)

          [,1]      [,2]      [,3]
[1,] 0.9733333 0.4444444 0.4722222
[2,] 0.4037037 0.8833333 0.5388889

# Token reordering — two of three tokens match exactly, the third is close
jaro_winkler_tokens("Kyle John Haynes", "John Kylie Haynes")

[1] 0.9844444

# Punctuation/spacing variants of the same name
jaro_winkler_tokens(c("OBrien", "OBrien"), c("O Brien", "O'Brien"))

[1] 1 1


The full mechanics of how jaro_winkler_tokens() resolves reordered tokens — and the extra_penalty argument for handling a stray extra token — are in Chapter 9 and the function reference (Chapter 11).

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
2.9 Edit distance
levenshtein(), osa_distance(), damerau_levenshtein(), and hamming() cover plain edits, restricted adjacent transpositions, unrestricted Damerau-Levenshtein, and position-wise differences. Existing APIs compare bytes by default; set use_bytes = FALSE for UTF-8 code points.

levenshtein("kitten", "sitting")

[1] 3

osa_distance("ca", "abc")             # 3 under the OSA restriction

[1] 3

damerau_levenshtein("ca", "abc")      # 2 under unrestricted DL

[1] 2

levenshtein_similarity("kitten", "sitting")

[1] 0.5714286

levenshtein_within("kitten", "sitting", max_distance = 3)

[1] TRUE

hamming("karolin", "kathrin")

[1] 3

hamming("abc", "ab")             # Inf for unequal length, matching stringdist

[1] Inf

title: 2  Quickstart
section: 2.10 Fuzzy lookup without a full matrix
text:
2.10 Fuzzy lookup without a full matrix
fuzzy_match() and fuzzy_top_n() scan a candidate table while retaining only the requested matches. They default to Unicode code-point comparison and avoid the potentially enormous all-pairs matrix.

choices <- c("SMYTH", "JONAS", "JONES", "MITTEN", "SITTING")
fuzzy_match(c("SMITH", "JONES"), choices)

[1] 1 3

fuzzy_top_n("kitten", choices, method = "levenshtein", top_n = 2)

  query_index table_index score rank
1           1           1     0    1
2           1           2     0    2

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
2.11 Candidate pairs and entity clusters
block_pairs() and sorted_neighbourhood() generate candidate pairs from one or more keys without comparing every pair, and cluster_pairs() turns the pairs you accept into one identifier per entity (Chapter 6).

surname <- c("SMITH", "SMYTH", "JONES", "SMITHE")
p <- block_pairs(soundex(surname))
p

  x_index y_index pass
1       1       2    1
2       1       4    1
3       2       4    1

sorted_neighbourhood(surname, window = 3)

  x_index y_index pass
1       1       3    1
2       1       4    1
3       2       4    1

cluster_pairs(p, n = length(surname))

[1] 1 1 2 1

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
2.12 Q-gram similarity
jaccard_index(), dice_coefficient(), tversky_index(), and cosine_similarity() compare two strings’ overlapping length-q substrings (“q-grams”) rather than their character-by-character alignment — insensitive to where a difference occurs, which makes them a useful second signal alongside Jaro-Winkler/edit-distance.

jaccard_index("night", "nacht")

[1] 0.1428571

dice_coefficient("night", "nacht")     # weights shared q-grams more heavily

[1] 0.25

tversky_index("night", "nacht", alpha = 1, beta = 1)  # == jaccard_index()

[1] 0.1428571


tversky_index() generalises the first two: alpha = beta = 1 is Jaccard, alpha = beta = 0.5 is Dice, and asymmetric weights are useful when one side is a query and the other a reference and the two kinds of mismatch shouldn’t be penalised equally.
cosine_similarity() is the one that isn’t a set metric. The other three reduce each string to a set of distinct q-grams, so a repeated q-gram counts once; cosine keeps the frequency profile and compares it as a vector, so repetition carries weight:

a <- c("aaaa", "BANANA", "night")
b <- c("aaab", "BANANAS", "nacht")
data.frame(a, b,
           jaccard = jaccard_index(a, b),
           dice    = dice_coefficient(a, b),
           cosine  = cosine_similarity(a, b))

       a       b   jaccard      dice    cosine
1   aaaa    aaab 0.5000000 0.6666667 0.8944272
2 BANANA BANANAS 0.7500000 0.8571429 0.9486833
3  night   nacht 0.1428571 0.2500000 0.2500000


"aaaa"/"aaab" share only the bigram "aa" out of two distinct bigrams — Jaccard 0.5 — but that bigram occurs three times on one side and twice on the other, which cosine sees and Jaccard cannot. Repetition like this is common in the numeric and code-like fields ("0000", "AAA-111") that sit next to names in a linkage file.

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
2.13 RapidFuzz scorers
fuzz_ratio(), fuzz_partial_ratio(), the token ratios, fuzz_wratio() and the rest are vectorised ports of the scorers in Python’s RapidFuzz, the maintained successor to fuzzywuzzy. Their scores agree with rapidfuzz.fuzz to floating-point precision, which makes them the natural choice when porting a matching pipeline from Python. All return 0-100. With full_process = TRUE (the default) both strings are lowercased and stripped of punctuation first, as RapidFuzz’s processor = default_process does.

fuzz_ratio("this is a test", "this is a test!")

[1] 100

fuzz_partial_ratio("fuzzy wuzzy was a bear", "wuzzy fuzzy was a bear")

[1] 93.02326

fuzz_token_sort_ratio("fuzzy was a bear", "bear was a fuzzy")

[1] 100

fuzz_token_set_ratio("fuzzy was a bear", "fuzzy fuzzy bear was a bear")

[1] 100

fuzz_wratio("New York Mets", "The New York Mets baseball club")

[1] 90


fuzz_extract() and fuzz_extract_one() port RapidFuzz’s process.extract() and extractOne(). They find each query’s best matches in a table, scoring in parallel and pruning candidates that cannot make the list.

teams <- c("Atlanta Falcons", "New York Jets", "New York Giants",
           "Dallas Cowboys")
fuzz_extract("new york jets", teams, limit = 2)

  query_index choice_index          choice     score rank
1           1            2   New York Jets 100.00000    1
2           1            3 New York Giants  78.57143    2

fuzz_extract_one(c("cowboys", "falcon"), teams)

           choice score choice_index
1  Dallas Cowboys    90            4
2 Atlanta Falcons    90            1

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
2.14 Putting it together
A typical pipeline profiles the input with fcount(), parses dates and load timestamps with fas.Date()/fas.POSIXct(), normalises with fchartr()/ftrimws(), builds blocking keys with refined_soundex()/cologne()/format_date(), scores candidates within each block with jaro_winkler_tokens() and cosine_similarity(), and stamps the result with format_datetime(). Chapter 10 walks through exactly that, end to end, on a small linkage example, and the use-case chapters (Chapter 3 to Chapter 8) take each stage further – including a deduplication of 100,000 records with block_pairs(), jaro_winkler() and cluster_pairs() in well under a second (Chapter 6).

title: 3  Clean and standardise text
text:
3.1 Web residue: entities, escapes and odd spaces
Most matching problems are really cleaning problems. Two records for the same business rarely differ by a typo; they differ by & against &, St. against Street, Müller against Mueller, or a postcode that lost its leading zero on the way through a spreadsheet. This chapter collects the functions that remove that noise, each of them one vectorised, multi-core call.
Text that has passed through a web page, a CMS export or a JSON API often arrives with HTML character references still in it, and with non-breaking or ideographic spaces where you expect ordinary ones. html_unescape() decodes every named and numeric reference of the HTML standard – exactly as Python’s html.unescape() does – and fsquish() trims and collapses every kind of Unicode whitespace:
scraped <- c("  Caf\u00e9\u00a0Nero ", "Fish & Chips\tCo.",
             "O\u2019Brien – Plumbing", "M\u00fcller\u3000GmbH",
             "Smith & Sons", "PLAIN NAME")
fsquish(html_unescape(scraped))

[1] "Café Nero"          "Fish & Chips Co."   "O’Brien – Plumbing" "Müller GmbH"        "Smith & Sons"       "PLAIN NAME"
  decodes to a non-breaking space, which is why fsquish() runs second. Strings without an & are returned untouched (not even copied), so running html_unescape() over a column that is mostly clean costs almost nothing.
Web logs and exported URLs carry percent-encoding instead. Pull out the part you need with fextract() and decode it; plus = TRUE treats + as a space, as HTML forms encode it:
logs <- c("/search?q=fish+%26+chips&page=2", "/search?q=caf%C3%A9+latte",
          "/search?page=1&q=100%25+beef", "/about")
q <- fextract("[?&]q=([^&]*)", logs, group = 1)
data.frame(q, decoded = url_decode(q, plus = TRUE))

                q      decoded
1  fish+%26+chips fish & chips
2 caf%C3%A9+latte   café latte
3     100%25+beef    100% beef
4            <NA>         <NA>
url_encode() goes the other way, with reserved = TRUE for a single query value. Both agree with utils::URLencode()/URLdecode() – except that a broken escape such as %zz is kept as it is rather than turned into garbage – and are several hundred times faster, because the base functions loop over characters in R code.

title: 3  Clean and standardise text
text:
3.2 Accents and typographic symbols
Names keyed on different systems disagree about accents: one has François Müller, another Francois Muller. ascii_fold() applies the same Latin-to-ASCII transliteration as ICU (and stringi), including ligatures, Nordic letters and typographic punctuation:

names <- c("Fran\u00e7ois M\u00fcller", "Zo\u00eb \u00c6lfric",
           "Bj\u00f6rk Gu\u00f0mundsd\u00f3ttir", "\u0141\u00f3d\u017a",
           "\u201cQuoted\u201d \u2013 dash", "\u00bd price \u2026")
data.frame(names, folded = ascii_fold(names))

                 names               folded
1      François Müller      Francois Muller
2           Zoë Ælfric          Zoe AElfric
3 Björk Guðmundsdóttir Bjork Gudmundsdottir
4                 Łódź                 Lodz
5      “Quoted” – dash      "Quoted" - dash
6            ½ price …        1/2 price ...


Characters with no ASCII spelling (other scripts, emoji) are kept, or replaced with sub when the output must be pure ASCII:

ascii_fold("Tokyo \u6771\u4eac caf\u00e9", sub = "?")

[1] "Tokyo ?? cafe"


The phonetic codes (soundex(), nysiis() and the rest) already fold accented letters internally; fold explicitly before the similarity functions and before hashing, where é and e would otherwise differ.

title: 3  Clean and standardise text
text:
3.3 Standardise words with a dictionary
Abbreviations are the biggest single source of disagreement in addresses and organisation names. freplace_tokens() replaces every whitespace- separated token found in a dictionary, in one hashed pass per string. An empty replacement deletes the token, and the result comes back squished. Strip the punctuation that clings to tokens first:

addr <- c("12 Smith St.", "3/45 North Rd", "UNIT 7, 9 KING STREET",
          "Flat 2 18 Queen st", "U 5/22 the Esplanade Hwy")
abbrev <- data.frame(
    from = c("ST", "RD", "AVE", "HWY", "CRES", "PDE", "FLAT", "U"),
    to   = c("STREET", "ROAD", "AVENUE", "HIGHWAY", "CRESCENT", "PARADE",
             "UNIT", "UNIT")
)
std <- freplace_tokens(fgsub("[.,]+", " ", toupper(addr)), abbrev$from, abbrev$to)
data.frame(addr, std)

                      addr                             std
1             12 Smith St.                 12 SMITH STREET
2            3/45 North Rd                 3/45 NORTH ROAD
3    UNIT 7, 9 KING STREET            UNIT 7 9 KING STREET
4       Flat 2 18 Queen st          UNIT 2 18 QUEEN STREET
5 U 5/22 the Esplanade Hwy UNIT 5/22 THE ESPLANADE HIGHWAY


Only whole tokens change – ST becomes STREET, but STAR and STREET itself are left alone – which is what makes a dictionary approach safe where gsub("ST", "STREET", x) is not. Matching can ignore ASCII case, and replacements may contain several words. The same mechanism maps name variants to one canonical form, here a (very) short nickname table:

nick <- data.frame(
    from = c("BILL", "BILLY", "WILL", "BOB", "ROB", "BOBBY", "PEG", "PEGGY",
             "LIZ", "BETH"),
    to   = c("WILLIAM", "WILLIAM", "WILLIAM", "ROBERT", "ROBERT", "ROBERT",
             "MARGARET", "MARGARET", "ELIZABETH", "ELIZABETH")
)
freplace_tokens(c("BILL", "Bob", "peggy", "WILLIAM", "LIZ ANNE"),
                nick$from, nick$to, ignore_case = TRUE)

[1] "WILLIAM"        "ROBERT"         "MARGARET"       "WILLIAM"        "ELIZABETH ANNE"


Dictionaries of thousands of entries cost no more per token than a dictionary of ten, because each token is one hash lookup. The equivalent in base R splits every string into a list, matches and pastes back:

set.seed(1)
n <- 2e5
words <- c("12", "SMITH", "ST", "RD", "AVE", "UNIT", "MR", "DR", "JOHN",
           "NORTH", "QLD", "4000")
x <- vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) paste(sample(words, 5, TRUE), collapse = " "), "")

system.time(freplace_tokens(x, abbrev$from, abbrev$to))

   user  system elapsed 
   0.14    0.02    0.06 

system.time({
    tok <- strsplit(x, " ", fixed = TRUE)
    vapply(tok, function(t) {
        m <- match(t, abbrev$from)
        t[!is.na(m)] <- abbrev$to[m[!is.na(m)]]
        paste(t, collapse = " ")
    }, "")
})

   user  system elapsed 
   1.79    0.14    1.92

title: 3  Clean and standardise text
text:
3.4 Restore leading zeros
Spreadsheets and CSV readers turn postcodes, phone numbers and identifiers into numbers and silently drop their leading zeros – every Northern Territory postcode (0800-0899) comes back as three digits. fpad() puts them back; side = "right" pads text for fixed-width exports:

fpad(as.character(c(800, 810, 2000, 4000, 870)), 4, pad = "0")

[1] "0800" "0810" "2000" "4000" "0870"

fpad(c("ID", "NAME", "POSTCODE"), 10, side = "right")

[1] "ID        " "NAME      " "POSTCODE  "


Width counts characters, not bytes, so accented text pads correctly too.

title: 3  Clean and standardise text
text:
3.5 Find the spelling variants
Before matching against anything else, it helps to know how many ways one value is spelled within a column. OpenRefine’s key collision clustering does this with a fingerprint: lower-case, fold accents, remove punctuation, then sort the unique words. Values that share a fingerprint are almost always the same thing:

companies <- c("Acme Pty Ltd", "ACME PTY. LTD.", "Ltd Acme Pty", "acme pty ltd ",
               "Acme Holdings", "Bolt & Nut Co", "Bolt and Nut Co",
               "Bolt & Nut Co.", "Cafe Nero", "Caf\u00e9 Nero")
key <- fingerprint(companies)
clusters <- split(companies, key)
clusters[lengths(clusters) > 1]

$`acme ltd pty`
[1] "Acme Pty Ltd"   "ACME PTY. LTD." "Ltd Acme Pty"   "acme pty ltd " 

$`bolt co nut`
[1] "Bolt & Nut Co"  "Bolt & Nut Co."

$`cafe nero`
[1] "Cafe Nero" "Café Nero"


"Bolt and Nut Co" stays out, because the fingerprint deletes & but keeps and. A dictionary pass first fixes that, which is the general pattern: standardise with freplace_tokens(), then cluster:

key2 <- fingerprint(freplace_tokens(companies, "and", "&", ignore_case = TRUE))
split(companies, key2)[["bolt co nut"]]

[1] "Bolt & Nut Co"   "Bolt and Nut Co" "Bolt & Nut Co." 


ngram_fingerprint() sorts the unique character n-grams instead of words, so it also joins values that differ by spacing or transposed letters (n = 1 is the most forgiving):

ngram_fingerprint(c("Cafe Nero", "CafeNero", "Cafe Neor"), n = 1)

[1] "acefnor" "acefnor" "acefnor"


Use the clusters to build the dictionary for freplace_tokens(), or as a deduplication key in their own right.

title: 3  Clean and standardise text
text:
3.6 A cleaning pipeline
In practice these run as one function applied to each name or address column before blocking and scoring:

clean_name <- function(x) {
    x <- html_unescape(x)
    x <- ascii_fold(x)
    x <- toupper(x)
    x <- fgsub("[^A-Z0-9 ]+", " ", x)
    x <- freplace_tokens(x, c(nick$from, "DR", "MR", "MRS", "MS"),
                         c(nick$to, "", "", "", ""))
    fsquish(x)
}
clean_name(c("  Dr. Fran\u00e7ois  O\u2019Brien-Smith ", "MR BILL  JONES",
             "bob jones"))

[1] "FRANCOIS O BRIEN SMITH" "WILLIAM JONES"          "ROBERT JONES"          


Every step is parallel and returns unchanged strings without copying them, so a pipeline like this keeps up with the matching steps that follow (Chapter 6) even at millions of rows.

title: 4  Find, flag and extract
text:
4.1 Flag records that mention any of many terms
Free-text fields hide structured values – a postcode at the end of an address, an amount in a description, a drug name in a case note. This chapter is about getting them out: flagging records that mention any of a long list of terms, tolerating misspellings, and extracting fields and numbers in one vectorised pass.
Keyword lists are long – medicines, product codes, place names, sanctions lists – and the obvious approaches scale badly: one grepl() per term reads the text once per term, and a single alternation of thousands of terms is slow for a backtracking regex engine. fgrepl_any() and its siblings build an Aho-Corasick automaton from the terms and read each string once, however many terms there are:
notes <- c("Pt given paracetamol 500mg and ibuprofen",
           "Reports nausea after AMOXICILLIN course",
           "No medication. Seen by police at home",
           "Advised to stop taking aspirin; started warfarin",
           "paracetemol 1g PRN",
           "Discussed diet and exercise")
drugs <- c("paracetamol", "ibuprofen", "amoxicillin", "aspirin", "warfarin",
           "ice", "codeine")

data.frame(
    any   = fgrepl_any(drugs, notes, ignore.case = TRUE),
    first = drugs[fwhich_any(drugs, notes, ignore.case = TRUE)],
    count = fcount_any(drugs, notes, ignore.case = TRUE)
)

    any       first count
1  TRUE paracetamol     2
2  TRUE amoxicillin     1
3  TRUE         ice     1
4  TRUE     aspirin     2
5 FALSE        <NA>     0
6 FALSE        <NA>     0
fwhich_any() reports the first term in the list that occurs, so the order of terms is a priority order – put the most specific or most serious terms first. fextract_any(all = TRUE) lists every occurrence.
Two things stand out. The terms are matched as substrings, so "ice" (the street name for methamphetamine) is found inside "police". Pad both sides with spaces to match whole words only:
as_words <- function(s) paste0(" ", fsquish(fgsub("[^[:alnum:]]+", " ", s)), " ")
fextract_any(paste0(" ", drugs, " "), as_words(notes), all = TRUE,
             ignore.case = TRUE)

[[1]]
[1] " paracetamol " " ibuprofen "  

[[2]]
[1] " AMOXICILLIN "

[[3]]
character(0)

[[4]]
[1] " aspirin "  " warfarin "

[[5]]
character(0)

[[6]]
character(0)
And "paracetemol" is misspelled, so no exact method finds it – that is the next section.
The speed difference is large even for a modest list. Here are 100,000 notes against 2,007 terms:
set.seed(2)
n <- 1e5
vocab <- c(drugs, "patient", "reviewed", "today", "pain", "mg", "daily",
           "home", "police", "nurse")
big <- vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) paste(sample(vocab, 8, TRUE), collapse = " "), "")
terms <- c(drugs, vapply(1:2000, function(i) paste(sample(letters, 8, TRUE), collapse = ""), ""))

system.time(hit_fast <- fgrepl_any(terms, big))

   user  system elapsed 
   0.00    0.00    0.02 

system.time(hit_base <- grepl(paste(terms, collapse = "|"), big))

   user  system elapsed 
  20.06    0.43   20.53 

identical(hit_fast, hit_base)

[1] TRUE

title: 4  Find, flag and extract
text:
4.2 Allow for typos
fagrepl() is agrepl() – the same arguments and the same results – computed with Myers’ bit-parallel algorithm on every core. It finds the pattern anywhere in each string within max.distance edits:

fagrepl("paracetamol", notes, max.distance = 2, ignore.case = TRUE)

[1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

identical(fagrepl("paracetamol", notes, max.distance = 2, ignore.case = TRUE),
          agrepl("paracetamol", notes, max.distance = 2, ignore.case = TRUE))

[1] TRUE


For a list of terms, call it once per term; it is fast enough that a few hundred terms over a million notes is practical. When the question is “which dictionary entry is this whole value closest to”, use fuzzy_within() instead (Chapter 6).

title: 4  Find, flag and extract
text:
4.3 Extract values with regular expressions
fextract() returns the first match per string, or one capture group of it; fextract_all() returns every match. Here are the state and postcode at the end of an Australian address:

addr <- c("12 Smith St, Brisbane QLD 4000", "Unit 3, 45 North Rd, Darwin NT 0800",
          "PO Box 99, Hobart TAS 7001", "No postcode here")
data.frame(
    state    = fextract("\\b(NSW|QLD|VIC|SA|WA|TAS|NT|ACT)\\s+[0-9]{4}$", addr, group = 1),
    postcode = fextract("\\b(NSW|QLD|VIC|SA|WA|TAS|NT|ACT)\\s+([0-9]{4})$", addr, group = 2)
)

  state postcode
1   QLD     4000
2    NT     0800
3   TAS     7001
4  <NA>     <NA>


And every phone number or email address in a message:

msg <- c("Call 0412 345 678 or 07 3123 4567", "email a.b@x.com, c@y.org", "nothing")
fextract_all("0[0-9][0-9 ]{7,11}[0-9]", msg)

[[1]]
[1] "0412 345 678" "07 3123 4567"

[[2]]
character(0)

[[3]]
character(0)

fextract_all("[[:alnum:]._]+@[[:alnum:].]+\\.[a-z]+", msg)

[[1]]
character(0)

[[2]]
[1] "a.b@x.com" "c@y.org"  

[[3]]
character(0)


Patterns follow the same rules as fgrepl(): base R’s extended regular expressions by default, PCRE with perl = TRUE, literal text with fixed = TRUE. Strings with no match give NA (or character(0) from fextract_all()), so the result lines up with the input row for row.

title: 4  Find, flag and extract
text:
4.4 Split delimited fields
fsplit_field() returns one field of delimited text without building the list that strsplit() would, which matters when you only want one or two fields of millions of rows:

full <- c("SMITH, John Paul", "O'BRIEN, Mary", "NGUYEN,Van  Anh", "MADONNA")
data.frame(full,
           surname = fsplit_field(full, ",", 1, fixed = TRUE),
           given   = fsquish(fsplit_field(full, ",", 2, fixed = TRUE)))

              full surname     given
1 SMITH, John Paul   SMITH John Paul
2    O'BRIEN, Mary O'BRIEN      Mary
3  NGUYEN,Van  Anh  NGUYEN   Van Anh
4          MADONNA MADONNA      <NA>

codes <- c("QLD|4000|BRISBANE", "NSW|2000|SYDNEY|CBD", "VIC||MELBOURNE")
data.frame(state    = fsplit_field(codes, "|", 1, fixed = TRUE),
           postcode = fsplit_field(codes, "|", 2, fixed = TRUE),
           last     = fsplit_field(codes, "|", -1, fixed = TRUE))

  state postcode      last
1   QLD     4000  BRISBANE
2   NSW     2000       CBD
3   VIC          MELBOURNE


Every field counts, including empty ones ("VIC||MELBOURNE" has an empty postcode), and negative positions count from the end.

title: 4  Find, flag and extract
text:
4.5 Numbers inside text
Amounts typed into free-text or spreadsheet columns come with currency symbols, thousands separators, units and labels. fparse_number() finds the first number in each string and ignores the rest:

prices <- c("$1,234.50", "AUD 99", "12.5%", "approx. 3,000 kg", "-$45.10",
            "(1,200)", "N/A", "Free")
data.frame(prices,
           fparse_number = fparse_number(prices),
           readr = suppressWarnings(readr::parse_number(prices)),
           gsub  = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(gsub("[^0-9.-]", "", prices))))

            prices fparse_number  readr   gsub
1        $1,234.50        1234.5 1234.5 1234.5
2           AUD 99          99.0   99.0   99.0
3            12.5%          12.5   12.5   12.5
4 approx. 3,000 kg        3000.0     NA    0.3
5          -$45.10         -45.1     NA  -45.1
6          (1,200)        1200.0 1200.0 1200.0
7              N/A            NA     NA     NA
8             Free            NA     NA     NA


The common shortcut of deleting everything but digits fails as soon as the text contains another full stop ("approx." becomes 0.3). readr::parse_number() returns NA for that case and for a minus sign in front of a currency symbol, and (in our tests) rounds about a quarter of two-decimal amounts to a neighbouring double; fparse_number() returns exactly what as.numeric() gives for the number it finds. Accounting-style negatives such as "(1,200)" are read as positive by both, so test for the parentheses separately if your data uses them. Other conventions are one argument away:

fparse_number(c("1.234,50 \u20ac", "12,5 %", "1 234 567,89"),
              decimal_mark = ",", grouping_mark = c(".", " "))

[1]    1234.5      12.5 1234567.9

title: 4  Find, flag and extract
text:
4.6 Count things per record
fcount() counts matches per string, which turns data-quality rules into one vectorised call each – digits in a name field, or the number of words:

names <- c("JOHN SMITH", "KYLE 2", "UNKNOWN 0000", "MARY-JANE O'NEIL")
data.frame(names, digits = fcount("[0-9]", names), words = fcount("[^ ]+", names))

             names digits words
1       JOHN SMITH      0     2
2           KYLE 2      1     2
3     UNKNOWN 0000      4     2
4 MARY-JANE O'NEIL      0     2


Chapter 5 builds on this to profile whole columns.

title: 5  Profile and validate columns
text:
5.1 What formats are in this column?
Before a column is cleaned or matched on, it pays to know what is in it: which formats occur, how often, and which values cannot possibly be right. Two functions do most of that work. string_shape() reduces each value to its pattern of character classes, and valid_id() checks the check digits that most real-world identifiers carry. Together with fcount(), fparse_number() and the strict date parsers they make a quick, vectorised data-quality report.
string_shape() replaces upper-case letters with A, lower-case letters with a and digits with 9, and keeps everything else. Tabulating the shapes of a phone-number column shows its formats at a glance:
set.seed(3)
n <- 1e5
phone <- sprintf(
    sample(c("04%02d %03d %03d", "04%02d%03d%03d", "(07) %04d %04d",
             "+61 4%02d %03d %03d"), n, TRUE, prob = c(.5, .25, .15, .1)),
    sample.int(99, n, TRUE), sample.int(999, n, TRUE), sample.int(999, n, TRUE)
)
phone[sample(n, 40)] <- sample(c("unknown", "N/A", "0412 345 67",
                                 "call after 5pm", "1234"), 40, TRUE)

shape <- string_shape(phone)
sort(table(shape), decreasing = TRUE)

shape
   9999 999 999      9999999999  (99) 9999 9999 +99 999 999 999     9999 999 99         aaaaaaa  aaaa aaaaa 9aa             A/A            9999 
          49944           25146           14763           10107              14               9               7               6               4
Four legitimate formats account for almost every row; everything with a small count deserves a look. The ten-digit mobile number that lost a digit (9999 999 99) is the kind of error no type check would catch:
rare <- names(which(table(shape) < 50))
unique(phone[shape %in% rare])

[1] "unknown"        "0412 345 67"    "N/A"            "call after 5pm" "1234"
collapse = TRUE reduces each run of one class to a single character, which groups values by structure rather than length – useful for free-text or name columns, where exact lengths vary:
string_shape(c("Smith", "SMITH", "O'Brien", "van der Berg", "J. Smith",
               "SMITH JNR", "Smith2"), collapse = TRUE)

[1] "Aa"     "A"      "A'Aa"   "a a Aa" "A. Aa"  "A A"    "Aa9"
Postcodes show how much a shape reveals with no domain rules at all – the letter O typed for a zero, a lost leading zero, a stray state or trailing space:
pc <- c("4000", "0800", "800", "4OOO", "2000 ", "NSW 2000", "40000", NA)
data.frame(pc, shape = string_shape(pc))

        pc    shape
1     4000     9999
2     0800     9999
3      800      999
4     4OOO     9AAA
5    2000     9999 
6 NSW 2000 AAA 9999
7    40000    99999
8     <NA>     <NA>
Letters and digits are classified by their Unicode category, so accented and non-Latin letters count as letters and combining accents disappear into the letter they modify.

title: 5  Profile and validate columns
text:
5.2 Validate identifiers
Most identifiers that people key in carry a check digit, chosen so that the common typing errors – one wrong digit, two adjacent digits swapped – produce an invalid number. valid_id() checks them for the identifiers that come up most in Australian and international data, ignoring spaces and hyphens:

valid_id(c("51 824 753 556", "51 824 753 557", "5182475355"), "abn")

[1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE

valid_id(c("2123 45670 1", "2123 45671 1", "7123 45670 1"), "medicare")

[1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE

valid_id(c("123 456 782", "123 456 789", "12345678"), "tfn")

[1]  TRUE FALSE    NA

valid_id(c("4111 1111 1111 1111", "4111 1111 1111 1112"), "luhn")

[1]  TRUE FALSE

valid_id(c("978-0-306-40615-7", "0-8044-2957-X"), "isbn")

[1] TRUE TRUE

valid_id("GB82 WEST 1234 5698 7654 32", "iban")

[1] TRUE


An 8-digit TFN gives NA: the older numbers use different weights, which the ATO does not publish, so the function will not guess. Passing the check does not prove that a number was ever issued – only that it is not a mistyped version of one.
To see how much this catches, take 5,000 well-formed ABNs, introduce a one-digit typo into 150 of them and blank out 30:

set.seed(4)
cand <- sprintf("%011.0f", floor(runif(1e6, 1e10, 1e11)))
abn <- head(cand[valid_id(cand, "abn")], 5000)   # about 1 in 89 is valid
abn <- ifelse(runif(5000) < 0.5,
              sub("^(..)(...)(...)(...)$", "\\1 \\2 \\3 \\4", abn), abn)
typo <- sample(5000, 150)
substr(abn[typo], 5, 5) <- as.character(sample(0:9, 150, TRUE))
abn[sample(5000, 30)] <- NA

table(valid = valid_id(abn, "abn"), useNA = "ifany")

valid
FALSE  TRUE  <NA> 
  131  4839    30 


Every invalid value is a typo, and every typo that changed a digit is invalid: ABN’s mod-89 check catches any single wrong digit. The typos it “missed” put back the digit that was already there, or landed on a row that was then blanked. Generating a million candidates and keeping the valid ones, as above, is itself a vectorised call that takes a fraction of a second.

title: 5  Profile and validate columns
text:
5.3 A column profile
Put together, a few vectorised calls give a one-row summary per column that is cheap enough to run on every column of every extract:

profile_column <- function(x, id_type = NULL) {
    x <- as.character(x)
    shapes <- sort(table(string_shape(x, collapse = TRUE)), decreasing = TRUE)
    data.frame(
        n         = length(x),
        missing   = mean(is.na(x) | !nzchar(fsquish(x))),
        distinct  = length(unique(x)),
        shapes    = length(shapes),
        top_shape = names(shapes)[1],
        top_share = round(as.numeric(shapes[1]) / sum(!is.na(x)), 3),
        valid     = if (is.null(id_type)) NA
                    else round(mean(valid_id(x, id_type), na.rm = TRUE), 3)
    )
}
rbind(cbind(column = "phone", profile_column(phone)),
      cbind(column = "abn", profile_column(abn, "abn")))

  column      n missing distinct shapes top_shape top_share valid
1  phone 100000   0.000    98851      7     9 9 9     0.500    NA
2    abn   5000   0.006     4971      2   9 9 9 9     0.502 0.974


Extend it with whatever rules matter for the data: fcount("[0-9]", x) for digits in name fields, is.na(fparse_number(x)) for amounts that do not parse, is.na(fas.Date(x, "dmy")) for impossible dates (Chapter 10 shows the date parsers used this way).

title: 6  Match, deduplicate and link records
text:
6.1 Candidate pairs by blocking
Record linkage – finding the records that refer to the same person, business or address, within one file or across several – has the same shape whatever the data:
Chapter 10 walks through a small linkage end to end. This chapter is the toolbox for each stage, and finishes by deduplicating 100,000 records.
Comparing every record with every other is \(O(n^2)\): five billion pairs for 100,000 records. Blocking only pairs records that agree exactly on a key, such as the Soundex code of the surname plus the date of birth. One key misses every true match with an error in that key, so linkage projects run several passes with different keys and take the union. block_pairs() does that in one call, with one column per pass, and reports each pair once along with the first pass that found it:
people <- data.frame(
    surname  = c("SMITH", "SMYTH", "JONES", "SMITH", "JONSE", "BROWN", "SMITH-JONES"),
    given    = c("JOHN", "JON", "MARY", "JOHN", "MARY", "ROBERT", "MARY"),
    dob      = as.Date(c("1980-01-02", "1980-01-02", "1975-06-30", "1990-12-01",
                         "1975-06-30", "1962-03-03", "1975-03-06")),
    postcode = c("4000", "4000", "2000", "4101", "2000", "3000", "2000")
)
keys <- data.frame(
    surname_dob = paste(soundex(people$surname), people$dob),
    dob         = people$dob,
    initial_pc  = paste(substr(people$given, 1, 1), people$postcode)
)
block_pairs(keys)

  x_index y_index pass
1       1       2    1
2       3       5    1
3       3       7    3
4       5       7    3
Record 7 – Mary Jones after a double-barrelled marriage, with day and month swapped in her date of birth – only shares the third key with records 3 and 5, and the pass column shows it. That makes a blocking design auditable: you can see which pass carries the recall, and drop the ones that only add noise. A missing key (NA) never pairs, and max_block_size skips blocks too big to be useful, such as the most common surname, with a warning.
Linking two files instead of deduplicating one is the same call with a second set of keys: block_pairs(keys_a, keys_b) returns pairs with one record from each.
crumbs: 6  Match, deduplicate and link records

title: 6  Match, deduplicate and link records
text:
6.2 The sorted neighbourhood method
Exact keys miss pairs whose keys differ in the last characters (SMITH and SMITHE). sorted_neighbourhood() sorts the distinct key values and pairs records whose values are within (window - 1) / 2 places of each other, as well as records with equal values. A second pass on the reversed key catches errors at the start of the string:

surname <- c("SMITH", "SMITHE", "SMYTH", "JONES", "JONSON", "XMITH")
rev_str <- function(s) vapply(strsplit(s, NULL),
                              function(ch) paste(rev(ch), collapse = ""), "")
p <- sorted_neighbourhood(data.frame(surname, rev_str(surname)), window = 3)
data.frame(a = surname[p$x_index], b = surname[p$y_index], pass = p$pass)

       a      b pass
1  SMITH SMITHE    1
2  SMITH JONSON    1
3  SMITH  XMITH    2
4 SMITHE  SMYTH    1
5  SMYTH JONSON    2
6  SMYTH  XMITH    1
7  JONES JONSON    1


XMITH only meets SMITH in the reversed pass. The window moves over distinct values, as in Python’s recordlinkage package, so the pairs do not depend on the order of the records and every tie is paired. Keys can be dates or numbers too: a date of birth with window = 3 pairs dates one day apart.
crumbs: 6  Match, deduplicate and link records

title: 6  Match, deduplicate and link records
section: 6.3 Choose phonetic keys by how much they merge
text:
6.3 Choose phonetic keys by how much they merge
Every phonetic code merges some spellings and separates others, and the trade-off is block size against recall. Comparing codes on a list of known variants shows the differences quickly:

surn <- c("SMITH", "SMYTH", "SCHMIDT", "MEYER", "MEIER", "MCDONALD",
          "MACDONALD", "THOMPSON", "TOMSON", "NGUYEN", "NGYUEN", "PHILLIPS",
          "FILLIPS")
codes <- data.frame(name = surn, soundex = soundex(surn), nysiis = nysiis(surn),
                    metaphone = metaphone(surn), statcan = statcan(surn),
                    phonex = phonex(surn), onca = onca(surn),
                    mra = mra_encode(surn))
codes

        name soundex nysiis metaphone statcan phonex onca    mra
1      SMITH    S530   SNAT       SM0    SMTH   S530 S530   SMTH
2      SMYTH    S530   SNYT       SM0    SMTH   S530 S530  SMYTH
3    SCHMIDT    S530   SNAD      SKMT    SCHM   S253 S530 SCHMDT
4      MEYER    M600  MAYAR       MYR      MR   M600 M600    MYR
5      MEIER    M600    MAR        MR      MR   M600 M600     MR
6   MCDONALD    M235 MCDANA      MKTN    MCDN   M235 M235 MCDNLD
7  MACDONALD    M235 MCDANA      MKTN    MCDN   M235 M235 MCDNLD
8   THOMPSON    T512 TANPSA      0MPS    THMP   T512 T512 THMPSN
9     TOMSON    T525 TANSAN      TMSN    TMSN   T525 T525   TMSN
10    NGUYEN    N250 NGAYAN      NKYN     NGN   N250 N250   NGYN
11    NGYUEN    N250  NGYAN      NJYN     NGN   N250 N250   NGYN
12  PHILLIPS    P412  FALAP      FLPS    PHLP   F410 F410  PHLPS
13   FILLIPS    F412  FALAP      FLPS    FLPS   F410 F410   FLPS

sapply(codes[-1], function(k) length(unique(k)))   # fewer = coarser blocks

  soundex    nysiis metaphone   statcan    phonex      onca       mra 
        8        11        10         9         8         7        11 


Soundex merges SCHMIDT with SMITH but separates PHILLIPS from FILLIPS; Phonex and ONCA join the latter pair; NYSIIS and Metaphone separate more spellings, which makes smaller blocks and needs more passes. The Match Rating Approach is designed as a comparison rather than a key: mra_compare() says whether two names match under its rules.

mra_compare(c("SMITH", "BYRNE", "CATHERINE"), c("SMYTH", "BOERN", "KATHRYN"))

[1] TRUE TRUE TRUE
crumbs: 6  Match, deduplicate and link records

title: 6  Match, deduplicate and link records
text:
6.4 Candidates without blocking keys
When there is no good key, search for similar strings directly; none of these functions builds the full comparison matrix.
fuzzy_within() returns every table entry within k edits of each query, using SymSpell’s symmetric-delete index – the right tool for checking typed values against a reference list such as a street gazetteer:

set.seed(7)
streets <- unique(paste(
    sample(c("KING", "QUEEN", "GEORGE", "ELIZABETH", "ANN", "ADELAIDE", "WICKHAM",
             "BRUNSWICK", "LOGAN", "IPSWICH", "OXLEY", "SANDGATE", "GYMPIE",
             "STANLEY", "MAIN", "CHURCH", "STATION", "RIVER"), 4000, TRUE),
    sample(c("ST", "RD", "AVE", "TCE", "PDE", "LANE", "CT", "CRES"), 4000, TRUE)
))
q <- c("KIGN ST", "QUEEN SRT", "WICKAM TCE", "LOGAN RD")
w <- fuzzy_within(q, streets, max_distance = 2)
data.frame(query = q[w$query_index], match = streets[w$table_index],
           distance = w$distance)

        query       match distance
1     KIGN ST     KING ST        1
2     KIGN ST     KING CT        2
3   QUEEN SRT    QUEEN ST        1
4   QUEEN SRT    QUEEN CT        2
5   QUEEN SRT    QUEEN RD        2
6  WICKAM TCE WICKHAM TCE        1
7    LOGAN RD    LOGAN RD        0
8    LOGAN RD   LOGAN PDE        2
9    LOGAN RD    LOGAN ST        2
10   LOGAN RD    LOGAN CT        2


Results come ordered by distance, so the first row per query is the best. The result is exact – the same pairs as filtering a full osa_distance_matrix() – at a fraction of the cost for large tables.
For names that differ by whole words – organisations with and without THE, UNI for UNIVERSITY, an extra department – edit distance is the wrong measure. tfidf_match() compares TF-IDF-weighted character n-grams, so rare, informative words dominate and common ones barely count:

orgs <- c("UNIVERSITY OF QUEENSLAND", "QUEENSLAND UNIVERSITY OF TECHNOLOGY",
          "GRIFFITH UNIVERSITY", "QUEENSLAND HEALTH", "BRISBANE CITY COUNCIL",
          "LOGAN CITY COUNCIL", "UNIVERSITY OF SYDNEY")
qs <- c("THE UNIVERSITY OF QUEENSLAND", "QLD UNIVERSITY OF TECHNOLOGY",
        "BRISBANE CITY COUNCIL LIBRARIES", "GRIFFITH UNI", "SYDNEY UNIVERSITY")
data.frame(query = qs, match = orgs[tfidf_match(qs, orgs)])

                            query                               match
1    THE UNIVERSITY OF QUEENSLAND            UNIVERSITY OF QUEENSLAND
2    QLD UNIVERSITY OF TECHNOLOGY QUEENSLAND UNIVERSITY OF TECHNOLOGY
3 BRISBANE CITY COUNCIL LIBRARIES               BRISBANE CITY COUNCIL
4                    GRIFFITH UNI                 GRIFFITH UNIVERSITY
5               SYDNEY UNIVERSITY                UNIVERSITY OF SYDNEY

tfidf_top_n("QLD UNIVERSITY OF TECHNOLOGY", orgs, top_n = 3)

  query_index table_index     score rank
1           1           2 0.8001508    1
2           1           7 0.3253862    2
3           1           1 0.3249688    3


For long text – product descriptions, case notes, addresses with free-text additions – minhash_pairs() finds pairs whose q-gram sets probably overlap by at least threshold (Jaccard), using locality-sensitive hashing, and verifies each candidate exactly:

descr <- c("Stainless steel kettle 1.7 litre with auto shut-off and boil-dry protection",
           "Stainless steel kettle 1.7L with auto shut off and boil dry protection",
           "Cordless stick vacuum cleaner with HEPA filter and wall mount",
           "Cordless stick vacuum with HEPA filter, wall mount included",
           "Cast iron frying pan 28cm pre-seasoned")
minhash_pairs(descr, threshold = 0.4)

  x_index y_index   jaccard
1       1       2 0.7195122
2       3       4 0.6197183
crumbs: 6  Match, deduplicate and link records

title: 6  Match, deduplicate and link records
section: 6.5 Score with the comparison that fits the field
text:
6.5 Score with the comparison that fits the field
Jaro-Winkler is the standard for short names, but each kind of field has its own kind of difference. Chapter 7 measures every comparator in the package against labelled name and address pairs and says which to reach for when; the short version is below:


Phonetic misspellings (PH/F, C/K) cost less under editex(), an edit distance whose substitution cost depends on whether the letters sound alike:

a <- c("PHILIP", "CATHERINE", "SHEPHERD")
b <- c("FILIP", "KATHRYN", "SHEPPARD")
data.frame(a, b, levenshtein = levenshtein_similarity(a, b),
           editex = editex_similarity(a, b))

          a        b levenshtein    editex
1    PHILIP    FILIP   0.6666667 0.7500000
2 CATHERINE  KATHRYN   0.5555556 0.7222222
3  SHEPHERD SHEPPARD   0.7500000 0.8125000




Multi-word names with reordered, missing or extra words suit monge_elkan() (the mean best match of each word) or jaro_winkler_tokens():

a <- c("JOHN PAUL SMITH", "MARY JANE O BRIEN", "ROBERT JONES")
b <- c("SMITH JOHN", "OBRIEN MARY", "BOB JONES")
data.frame(a, b, jaro_winkler = jaro_winkler(a, b),
           monge_elkan = monge_elkan(a, b), tokens = jaro_winkler_tokens(a, b))

                  a           b jaro_winkler monge_elkan    tokens
1   JOHN PAUL SMITH  SMITH JOHN    0.5000000   0.6666667 0.6666667
2 MARY JANE O BRIEN OBRIEN MARY    0.5659537   0.7986111 0.5666667
3      ROBERT JONES   BOB JONES    0.7060185   0.7888889 0.7500000




One string inside another – a street address inside a full address line – is local alignment: smith_waterman() scores the best-matching substring, and lcs_str() returns the longest common substring:

smith_waterman(c("9 KING ST", "9 KING ST"),
               c("UNIT 4 9 KING ST BRISBANE", "19 KINGS ST"))

[1] 1.0000000 0.9444444

lcs_str("9 KING ST", "UNIT 4 9 KING ST BRISBANE")

[1] "9 KING ST"




When a pair goes to clerical review, edit_ops() explains a distance as the edits themselves:

edit_ops("JONATHAN", "JONHATAN", type = "opcodes")

  pair   type a_start a_end b_start b_end
1    1  equal       1     3       1     3
2    1 insert       4     3       4     4
3    1  equal       4     5       5     6
4    1 delete       6     6       7     6
5    1  equal       7     8       7     8
crumbs: 6  Match, deduplicate and link records

title: 6  Match, deduplicate and link records
text:
6.6 From matched pairs to entities
Deduplication needs one identifier per entity, not a list of pairs. cluster_pairs() joins records connected by any chain of matches (the connected components of the match graph):

# 1 matches 2, 2 matches 3, 4 matches 5; record 6 matches nothing
cluster_pairs(c(1, 2, 4), c(2, 3, 5), n = 6)

[1] 1 1 1 2 2 3


Chaining is also the risk: if 1 and 3 do not match directly, the cluster rests on record 2. Look at the largest clusters before trusting them, or raise the threshold for pairs that join large clusters.
crumbs: 6  Match, deduplicate and link records

title: 6  Match, deduplicate and link records
text:
6.7 End to end: deduplicating 100,000 records
To see the whole pipeline at a useful scale, build a file of 80,000 people in which a quarter appear a second time with one error each: a typo in the surname or given name, a date of birth one day out, or a missing postcode.

set.seed(42)
surnames <- c("SMITH", "JONES", "WILLIAMS", "BROWN", "WILSON", "TAYLOR", "JOHNSON",
    "WHITE", "MARTIN", "ANDERSON", "THOMPSON", "NGUYEN", "THOMAS", "WALKER", "HARRIS",
    "LEE", "RYAN", "ROBINSON", "KELLY", "KING", "DAVIS", "WRIGHT", "EVANS", "ROBERTS",
    "GREEN", "HALL", "WOOD", "JACKSON", "CLARKE", "PATEL", "KHAN", "LEWIS", "JAMES",
    "PHILLIPS", "MITCHELL", "CAMPBELL", "MORRIS", "YOUNG", "SCOTT", "MURPHY", "COOK",
    "BAKER", "TURNER", "COOPER", "HILL", "WARD", "HUGHES", "MOORE", "CHEN", "WANG",
    "SINGH", "OBRIEN", "MCDONALD", "STEWART", "MACDONALD", "SULLIVAN", "MURRAY",
    "WATSON", "PRICE", "BELL", "ALLEN")
given <- c("JOHN", "MARY", "ROBERT", "JENNIFER", "MICHAEL", "LINDA", "WILLIAM",
    "ELIZABETH", "DAVID", "SUSAN", "JAMES", "MARGARET", "PETER", "SARAH", "ANDREW",
    "JESSICA", "DANIEL", "EMILY", "MATTHEW", "CHLOE", "THOMAS", "OLIVIA", "JOSHUA",
    "EMMA", "RYAN", "GRACE", "BENJAMIN", "SOPHIE", "LUKE", "HANNAH", "KYLE", "ZOE",
    "NATHAN", "AMY", "SAMUEL", "LUCY")
n_people <- 80000
truth <- data.frame(
    person   = seq_len(n_people),
    surname  = sample(surnames, n_people, TRUE),
    given    = sample(given, n_people, TRUE),
    dob      = as.Date("1940-01-01") + sample(0:25000, n_people, TRUE),
    postcode = sprintf("%04d", sample(c(800:899, 2000:4999), n_people, TRUE))
)

# One random substitution, deletion or transposition per string
typo <- function(s) {
    k <- nchar(s)
    i <- floor(runif(length(s)) * k) + 1
    r <- runif(length(s))
    out <- s
    sub_ <- r < 0.4
    substr(out[sub_], i[sub_], i[sub_]) <- sample(LETTERS, sum(sub_), TRUE)
    del <- r >= 0.4 & r < 0.7
    out[del] <- paste0(substr(s[del], 1, i[del] - 1), substr(s[del], i[del] + 1, 100))
    tr <- r >= 0.7 & i < k
    out[tr] <- paste0(substr(s[tr], 1, i[tr] - 1), substr(s[tr], i[tr] + 1, i[tr] + 1),
                      substr(s[tr], i[tr], i[tr]), substr(s[tr], i[tr] + 2, 100))
    out
}
copies <- truth[sample(n_people, n_people / 4), ]
e <- runif(nrow(copies))
copies$surname[e < 0.3] <- typo(copies$surname[e < 0.3])
copies$given[e >= 0.3 & e < 0.5] <- typo(copies$given[e >= 0.3 & e < 0.5])
off <- e >= 0.5 & e < 0.65
copies$dob[off] <- copies$dob[off] + sample(c(-1, 1), sum(off), TRUE)
copies$postcode[e >= 0.65 & e < 0.8] <- NA

records <- rbind(truth, copies)
records <- records[sample(nrow(records)), ]
nrow(records)

[1] 100000


Three blocking passes, each robust to a different kind of error: a phonetic surname with the date of birth (survives most surname typos), the given name with the date of birth (survives any surname change), and the exact names with the postcode (survives date errors):

system.time(
    pairs <- block_pairs(data.frame(
        surname_dob = paste(soundex(records$surname), records$dob),
        given_dob   = paste(records$given, records$dob),
        names_pc    = paste(records$surname, substr(records$given, 1, 1),
                            records$postcode)
    ))
)

   user  system elapsed 
   0.30    0.03    0.34 

nrow(pairs)

[1] 35763

table(pass = pairs$pass)

pass
    1     2     3 
17395  8201 10167 


Score each candidate on every field, weight them, and keep pairs above a threshold:

system.time({
    i <- pairs$x_index
    j <- pairs$y_index
    surname_sim <- jaro_winkler(records$surname[i], records$surname[j])
    given_sim   <- jaro_winkler(records$given[i], records$given[j])
    dob_agree   <- as.numeric(abs(records$dob[i] - records$dob[j]) <= 1)
    pc_agree    <- ifelse(is.na(records$postcode[i]) | is.na(records$postcode[j]), 0.5,
                          as.numeric(records$postcode[i] == records$postcode[j]))
    pairs$score <- (2 * surname_sim + given_sim + dob_agree + 0.5 * pc_agree) / 4.5
})

   user  system elapsed 
   0.01    0.00    0.00 

matches <- pairs[pairs$score >= 0.9, ]

Then cluster the matches into entities:

system.time(entity <- cluster_pairs(matches, n = nrow(records)))

   user  system elapsed 
      0       0       0 

c(entities = max(entity), true_people = n_people)

   entities true_people 
      80045       80000 

table(cluster_size = tabulate(entity))

cluster_size
    1     2     3     4 
60094 19948     2     1 


Because the data are synthetic we know the truth, so we can measure how well each stage did:

same_person <- function(a, b) records$person[a] == records$person[b]
true_pairs  <- sum(choose(table(records$person), 2))
c(
    blocking_recall = sum(same_person(pairs$x_index, pairs$y_index)) / true_pairs,
    precision       = mean(same_person(matches$x_index, matches$y_index)),
    recall          = sum(same_person(matches$x_index, matches$y_index)) / true_pairs
)

blocking_recall       precision          recall 
      1.0000000       0.9997996       0.9976000 


Blocking reduced five billion possible pairs to a few tens of thousands without losing a true match, and the whole run takes well under a second. The weights and threshold here are picked by hand; on real data, tune them against a labelled sample, or estimate them with a probabilistic model (the fastLink and reclin2 packages fit Fellegi-Sunter weights) and use fast.string for the steps around it.

title: 7  Choose a string metric
text:
7.1 The candidates
This package ships around thirty ways to score how alike two strings are. Picking one by reputation – “Jaro-Winkler is the standard for names” – leaves the obvious question unanswered: standard for which names, against which wrong answers?
This chapter answers it by measurement. Three hand-labelled sets of pairs, one each for given names, surnames and addresses, are scored by every candidate comparator, and the results say which comparator separates the true pairs from the false ones in each field. Every number below is computed when this page is rendered; the code is all here, so the same exercise runs on your own labelled pairs by swapping the data in.
Three things fall out of it, and they are worth stating before the tables:
comparators <- list(
    jaro_winkler   = function(a, b) jaro_winkler(a, b),
    jaro           = function(a, b) jaro_winkler(a, b, p = 0),
    jw_tokens      = function(a, b) jaro_winkler_tokens(a, b),
    monge_elkan    = function(a, b) monge_elkan(a, b, symmetric = TRUE),
    levenshtein    = function(a, b) levenshtein_similarity(a, b),
    osa            = function(a, b) osa_similarity(a, b),
    editex         = function(a, b) editex_similarity(a, b),
    indel          = function(a, b) indel_similarity(a, b),
    lcs_seq        = function(a, b) lcs_seq_similarity(a, b),
    lcs_str        = function(a, b) lcs_str_similarity(a, b),
    prefix         = function(a, b) prefix_similarity(a, b),
    smith_waterman = function(a, b) smith_waterman(a, b),
    jaccard_q2     = function(a, b) jaccard_index(a, b, q = 2),
    jaccard_q3     = function(a, b) jaccard_index(a, b, q = 3),
    cosine_q3      = function(a, b) cosine_similarity(a, b, q = 3),
    tversky_in     = function(a, b) tversky_index(a, b, q = 3, alpha = 1, beta = 0),
    fuzz_token_set = function(a, b) fuzz_token_set_ratio(a, b) / 100,
    fuzz_wratio    = function(a, b) fuzz_wratio(a, b) / 100,
    soundex_equal  = function(a, b) as.numeric(soundex(a) == soundex(b))
)
Every one is put on the same scale, where 1 means identical: the *_similarity() functions already are, the RapidFuzz scorers are divided by 100, and distances are left out in favour of their similarity twins. rLink() does this conversion itself, so a comparator chosen here drops straight into a linkage (Chapter 6).

The labels encode one judgement: would a reviewer, seeing only this field, call these the same person or address? Several pairs are genuinely arguable – THOMSON/THOMPSON is a misspelling as often as it is two families – and they are labelled non-match deliberately, because a comparator that cannot be told to be cautious there is a comparator that will merge two people. The non-match side is adversarial by design: half of it is near misses, where a real linkage would see mostly unrelated pairs. The absolute numbers below are therefore pessimistic; what they are good for is ranking the comparators against each other on the pairs that decide a linkage.

title: 7  Choose a string metric
text:
7.3 How each comparator is scored
Two measures, both reported per field:


AUC – the probability that a randomly chosen true pair outranks a randomly chosen false one, over the easy and moderate pairs only. It needs no threshold, which matters because the right threshold differs per comparator. The hard pairs are excluded here and reported separately, since (as the tables show) no comparator separates them and including them only compresses the ranking.

Mean score per cell of the match x degree grid, which is where the behaviour actually shows: a comparator is useful when its moderate matches sit well above its moderate non-matches.


score_all <- function(pairs) {
    scores <- lapply(comparators, function(f) f(pairs$a, pairs$b))
    cbind(pairs, as.data.frame(scores))
}

# Mann-Whitney / rank formulation: no bootstrapping, no ties problem
auc <- function(score, match) {
    r <- rank(score)
    n1 <- sum(match)
    n0 <- sum(!match)
    (sum(r[match]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

report <- function(pairs) {
    scored <- score_all(pairs)
    easy_mod <- scored$degree != "hard"
    cell <- function(v, keep) round(mean(v[keep]), 2)
    out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(comparators), function(nm) {
        v <- scored[[nm]]
        data.frame(
            comparator = nm,
            auc = round(auc(v[easy_mod], scored$match[easy_mod]), 2),
            tp_easy = cell(v, scored$match & scored$degree == "easy"),
            tp_mod  = cell(v, scored$match & scored$degree == "moderate"),
            tp_hard = cell(v, scored$match & scored$degree == "hard"),
            fp_easy = cell(v, !scored$match & scored$degree == "easy"),
            fp_mod  = cell(v, !scored$match & scored$degree == "moderate"),
            fp_hard = cell(v, !scored$match & scored$degree == "hard")
        )
    }))
    out$margin <- out$tp_mod - out$fp_mod
    out[order(-out$auc, -out$margin), ]
}

kable_report <- function(pairs, caption) {
    knitr::kable(
        report(pairs), row.names = FALSE, caption = caption,
        col.names = c("Comparator", "AUC", "easy", "moderate", "hard",
                      "easy", "moderate", "hard", "margin")
    )
}

In the tables, the first group of three columns is the mean score on true matches of each difficulty, the second group the mean on non-matches, and margin is the moderate gap between them – the headroom a threshold has to work in.
