fast.string::jaro_winkler_tokens 0.630s (7.0x the plain-comparison cost)

text:
12.6 Edit distance

t_fast_lv <- system.time(fast.string::levenshtein(names_x, rev(names_x)))["elapsed"]
t_fast_osa <- system.time(fast.string::osa_distance(names_x, rev(names_x)))["elapsed"]
t_fast_dl <- system.time(fast.string::damerau_levenshtein(names_x, rev(names_x)))["elapsed"]
cat(sprintf("fast.string::levenshtein         %.3fs\nfast.string::osa_distance        %.3fs\nfast.string::damerau_levenshtein %.3fs\n",
            t_fast_lv, t_fast_osa, t_fast_dl))

fast.string::levenshtein         0.170s
fast.string::osa_distance        0.170s
fast.string::damerau_levenshtein 0.230s

if (has_stringdist) {
    t_sd_lv <- system.time(stringdist::stringdist(names_x, rev(names_x), method = "lv"))["elapsed"]
    t_sd_osa <- system.time(stringdist::stringdist(names_x, rev(names_x), method = "osa"))["elapsed"]
    t_sd_dl <- system.time(stringdist::stringdist(names_x, rev(names_x), method = "dl"))["elapsed"]
    cat(sprintf("stringdist (lv) %.3fs\nstringdist (osa) %.3fs\nstringdist (dl) %.3fs\n", t_sd_lv, t_sd_osa, t_sd_dl))
    record("levenshtein", "stringdist::stringdist(lv)", t_sd_lv, t_fast_lv)
    record("osa_distance", "stringdist::stringdist(osa)", t_sd_osa, t_fast_osa)
    record("damerau_levenshtein", "stringdist::stringdist(dl)", t_sd_dl, t_fast_dl)
}

stringdist (lv) 0.340s
stringdist (osa) 0.360s
stringdist (dl) 0.530s

# hamming() needs equal-length pairs to avoid the all-Inf degenerate case
names_eqlen <- fast.string::fsubstr(names_x, 1, 8)
t_fast_hm <- system.time(fast.string::hamming(names_eqlen, rev(names_eqlen)))["elapsed"]
cat(sprintf("fast.string::hamming %.3fs\n", t_fast_hm))

fast.string::hamming 0.180s

if (has_stringdist) {
    t_sd_hm <- system.time(stringdist::stringdist(names_eqlen, rev(names_eqlen), method = "hamming"))["elapsed"]
    cat(sprintf("stringdist (hamming) %.3fs\n", t_sd_hm))
    record("hamming", "stringdist::stringdist(hamming)", t_sd_hm, t_fast_hm)
}

stringdist (hamming) 0.390s


fuzzy_match() computes the same best-match result without retaining the full score matrix. The output matrix below is modest for documentation, but its allocation grows as length(query) * length(table) while lookup output remains one integer per query.

lookup_queries <- names_x[seq_len(100L)]
lookup_table <- names_x[1001:2000]
t_lookup <- system.time(
    fuzzy_match(lookup_queries, lookup_table, use_bytes = TRUE)
)["elapsed"]
t_matrix <- system.time(
    max.col(jaro_winkler_matrix(lookup_queries, lookup_table),
            ties.method = "first")
)["elapsed"]
cat(sprintf("fuzzy_match %.3fs; materialized matrix %.3fs\n",
            t_lookup, t_matrix))

fuzzy_match 0.000s; materialized matrix 0.000s



# Each edit-distance implementation should agree with its stringdist method.
a3 <- c("kitten", "Saturday", "flaw")
b3 <- c("sitting", "Sunday", "lawn")
fast.string::levenshtein(a3, b3)

[1] 3 3 2

if (has_stringdist) stringdist::stringdist(a3, b3, method = "lv")

[1] 3 3 2

fast.string::osa_distance("ca", "abc")

[1] 3

if (has_stringdist) stringdist::stringdist("ca", "abc", method = "osa")

[1] 3

fast.string::damerau_levenshtein("ca", "abc")

[1] 2

if (has_stringdist) stringdist::stringdist("ca", "abc", method = "dl")

[1] 2

text:
12.7 Q-gram similarity

t_fast_jac <- system.time(fast.string::jaccard_index(names_x, rev(names_x)))["elapsed"]
cat(sprintf("fast.string::jaccard_index %.3fs\n", t_fast_jac))

fast.string::jaccard_index 0.200s

if (has_stringdist) {
    t_sd_jac <- system.time(stringdist::stringsim(names_x, rev(names_x), method = "jaccard"))["elapsed"]
    cat(sprintf("stringdist::stringsim(jaccard) %.3fs\n", t_sd_jac))
    record("jaccard_index", "stringdist::stringsim(jaccard)", t_sd_jac, t_fast_jac)
}

stringdist::stringsim(jaccard) 0.510s

t_fast_dice <- system.time(fast.string::dice_coefficient(names_x, rev(names_x)))["elapsed"]
t_fast_tver <- system.time(fast.string::tversky_index(names_x, rev(names_x), alpha = 0.3, beta = 0.7))["elapsed"]
cat(sprintf("fast.string::dice_coefficient %.3fs (no direct stringdist equivalent)\n", t_fast_dice))

fast.string::dice_coefficient 0.220s (no direct stringdist equivalent)

cat(sprintf("fast.string::tversky_index    %.3fs (no direct stringdist equivalent)\n", t_fast_tver))

fast.string::tversky_index    0.170s (no direct stringdist equivalent)


cosine_similarity() does strictly more work than the three set metrics — its q-gram vectors are sorted but not deduplicated, so the merge pass walks more elements and accumulates three running sums instead of one intersection count. stringdist::stringsim(method = "cosine") is the direct equivalent.

t_fast_cos <- system.time(fast.string::cosine_similarity(names_x, rev(names_x)))["elapsed"]
cat(sprintf("fast.string::cosine_similarity %.3fs\n", t_fast_cos))

fast.string::cosine_similarity 0.200s

if (has_stringdist) {
    t_sd_cos <- system.time(stringdist::stringsim(names_x, rev(names_x), method = "cosine", q = 2))["elapsed"]
    cat(sprintf("stringdist::stringsim(cosine)  %.3fs\n", t_sd_cos))
    record("cosine_similarity", "stringdist::stringsim(cosine)", t_sd_cos, t_fast_cos)
}

stringdist::stringsim(cosine)  1.660s

12.8 RapidFuzz scorers
The fuzz_*() ports of Python’s RapidFuzz scorers on the same multi-token names. None of the comparison packages here implements these scores, so this is absolute throughput only.

t_ratio   <- system.time(fast.string::fuzz_ratio(tok_a, tok_b))["elapsed"]
t_partial <- system.time(fast.string::fuzz_partial_ratio(tok_a, tok_b))["elapsed"]
t_tsort   <- system.time(fast.string::fuzz_token_sort_ratio(tok_a, tok_b))["elapsed"]
t_tset    <- system.time(fast.string::fuzz_token_set_ratio(tok_a, tok_b))["elapsed"]
t_wratio  <- system.time(fast.string::fuzz_wratio(tok_a, tok_b))["elapsed"]
cat(sprintf(
    "fast.string::fuzz_ratio            %.3fs\nfast.string::fuzz_partial_ratio    %.3fs\nfast.string::fuzz_token_sort_ratio %.3fs\nfast.string::fuzz_token_set_ratio  %.3fs\nfast.string::fuzz_wratio           %.3fs\n",
    t_ratio, t_partial, t_tsort, t_tset, t_wratio
))

fast.string::fuzz_ratio            0.140s
fast.string::fuzz_partial_ratio    0.320s
fast.string::fuzz_token_sort_ratio 0.180s

title: 12  Benchmarks at scale
section: 12.9 Text cleaning, extraction, validation and linkage
text:
12.9 Text cleaning, extraction, validation and linkage
The newer functions have the widest gaps, because their usual R equivalents are either loops over strings in R code, one regular expression per dictionary entry, or packages that call into C one string at a time. These run on 1 million strings (n_new below) of a shape that suits each task. A few baselines would take minutes at that size – utils::URLencode(), xml2 used to decode HTML, digest::digest() called per string, and a 1,000-term alternation – so they run on a sample and are scaled to n_new; the table marks those rows.

set.seed(2)
n_new <- 1e6
results_new <- list()
record_new <- function(op, baseline, baseline_s, fast_s, sampled = FALSE) {
    results_new[[length(results_new) + 1]] <<- data.frame(
        operation = op, baseline = baseline, scaled = if (sampled) "yes" else "",
        baseline_s = unname(baseline_s), fast_s = unname(fast_s),
        speedup = unname(baseline_s / fast_s)
    )
}
words <- c("12", "SMITH", "ST", "RD", "AVE", "UNIT", "MR", "DR", "JOHN",
           "NORTH", "QLD", "4000", "BRISBANE", "CRES", "HWY", "PDE")
addr <- do.call(paste, lapply(1:5, function(i) sample(words, n_new, TRUE)))


from <- c("ST", "RD", "AVE", "CRES", "HWY", "PDE", "MR", "DR")
to   <- c("STREET", "ROAD", "AVENUE", "CRESCENT", "HIGHWAY", "PARADE", "", "")
t_base <- system.time({
    tok <- strsplit(addr, " ", fixed = TRUE)
    vapply(tok, function(t) {
        m <- match(t, from); t[!is.na(m)] <- to[m[!is.na(m)]]
        paste(t[nzchar(t)], collapse = " ")
    }, "")
})["elapsed"]
t_stri <- system.time(stri_replace_all_regex(addr, paste0("\\b", from, "\\b"), to,
                                             vectorize_all = FALSE))["elapsed"]
t_fast <- system.time(freplace_tokens(addr, from, to))["elapsed"]
record_new("freplace_tokens (8 words)", "strsplit + match + paste", t_base, t_fast)
record_new("freplace_tokens (8 words)", "stringi regex, one per word", t_stri, t_fast)

pc <- as.character(sample(200:9999, n_new, TRUE))
t_stri <- system.time(stri_pad_left(pc, 4, "0"))["elapsed"]
t_fast <- system.time(fpad(pc, 4, pad = "0"))["elapsed"]
record_new("fpad", "stringi::stri_pad_left", t_stri, t_fast)

acc <- do.call(paste, lapply(1:3, function(i) sample(
    c("Fran\u00e7ois", "M\u00fcller", "Zo\u00eb", "caf\u00e9", "plain", "\u00c6sir"),
    n_new, TRUE)))
t_stri <- system.time(stri_trans_general(acc, "Latin-ASCII"))["elapsed"]
t_fast <- system.time(ascii_fold(acc))["elapsed"]
record_new("ascii_fold", "stringi Latin-ASCII", t_stri, t_fast)

ht <- rep(c("Tom & Jerry", "café é A", "a <b> c",
            "plain text"), length.out = n_new)
k <- 2000
t_base <- system.time(vapply(ht[1:k], function(s)
    xml2::xml_text(xml2::read_html(paste0("<p>", s, "</p>"))), ""))["elapsed"] * n_new / k
t_fast <- system.time(html_unescape(ht))["elapsed"]
record_new("html_unescape", "xml2, one string at a time", t_base, t_fast, sampled = TRUE)

u <- paste0("https://example.com/search?q=", stri_rand_strings(n_new, 20, "[a-z/\\&\\u0020]"))
k <- 10000
t_base <- system.time(URLencode(u[1:k], reserved = TRUE))["elapsed"] * n_new / k
t_curl <- system.time(curl::curl_escape(u))["elapsed"]
t_fast <- system.time(enc <- url_encode(u, reserved = TRUE))["elapsed"]

title: 12  Benchmarks at scale
text:
12.10 The small-n crossover
Chapter 9 claims every parallel function applies a size threshold and falls back to single-threaded execution below it, because thread-pool dispatch overhead would otherwise exceed the time saved. Here’s that claim checked directly, at n = 20 — small enough that the claim predicts fast.string will be no faster, possibly slower than base R:

small <- stri_rand_strings(20, sample(5:15, 20, replace = TRUE))
print(microbenchmark(
    base = base::grepl("[0-9]", small),
    fast = fast.string::fgrepl("[0-9]", small),
    times = 50
))

Unit: microseconds
 expr  min   lq   mean median   uq   max neval
 base  5.3  6.5 10.118   8.65 11.4  52.1    50
 fast 66.5 67.7 74.790  69.20 72.6 172.0    50


At this scale the two are within noise of each other (sometimes base R even wins outright) — exactly what the size-threshold design predicts, and the reason the rest of this chapter uses 3M rows rather than 20: the benefit this package offers only shows up once there’s enough work to amortise parallel dispatch.

A few patterns worth drawing out explicitly, in descending order of speedup:


The biggest wins aren’t parallelism wins at all. fas.POSIXct(), fas.Date(), format_date(), and fcount() land in the hundreds of times faster, and the reason is that they do less work, not that they spread the same work over more cores: no locale handling, no timezone database, no %-format interpretation, and — for fcount() — no per-element allocation of a match-position vector that gets discarded. These are the rows to read with the trade-off in mind: each one accepts a narrower contract (one fixed shape, no format guessing) in exchange, and Chapter 9 is explicit about where that narrowness bites.

Phonetic encoding and multi-pattern substitution are the genuine parallelism wins — roughly 8-60x, on operations with real per-element branching to spread across cores. cologne() and caverphone() sit at the top of that band mainly because their single-threaded R baselines are expensive.

The smallest wins are where the baseline is already tight C. The edit-distance and q-gram kernels against stringdist run 1.3-1.8x (damerau_levenshtein is actually slower here, at 0.8x), because stringdist is a well-optimised C implementation and there is little headroom beyond threading. Same story for substr() at 1.1x, which base R already does close to memcpy speed. cosine_similarity() is the exception in that group at 5.7x, since stringdist tabulates q-grams generically where this package packs them into integers.
Cross-package comparisons (stringdist, RecordLinkage, phonics) confirm correctness as much as speed — the Jaro-Winkler numbers agree to floating-point precision, cosine_similarity() matches stringdist’s cosine, and refined_soundex() matches phonics::refinedSoundex() once its truncation is disabled. Agreement is the more important result, since a faster-but-wrong implementation isn’t a useful trade. Where outputs don’t agree — cologne() versus phonics::cologne(), and the Soundex H/W rule — Chapter 9 says exactly which rule each side takes.

title: 13  Troubleshooting & FAQ
text: 13.1 Installation

title: 13  Troubleshooting & FAQ
text:
“could not find tools necessary to compile a package” / install fails
fast.string compiles C++ source on install (PCRE2 bindings, prepared literal search, RcppParallel). You need a working toolchain:


Windows: install Rtools matching your R version, and make sure it’s on PATH (the Rtools installer offers to do this). Verify with pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE).

macOS: install Xcode command-line tools (xcode-select --install) and PCRE2 (brew install pcre2).

Linux: a C++ compiler (gcc/clang) plus the PCRE2 development headers — libpcre2-dev on Debian/Ubuntu, pcre2-devel on Fedora/RHEL.

fast.string needs R 4.1.0 or later.
If pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE) returns FALSE, the underlying compiler invocation it prints is the fastest way to see exactly what’s missing.
Reinstalling after pulling new source changes
If you’re developing against a local checkout rather than installing a release, devtools::load_all() recompiles changed src/*.cpp files automatically; a plain library(fast.string) won’t pick up source changes without reinstalling first.

title: 13  Troubleshooting & FAQ
text:
13.2 NA, empty strings, and encoding
Why does my function return NA for a non-NA input?
Every function in this package returns NA for NA input — but a few functions also return NA for specific valid-looking but unparseable inputs:


soundex()/nysiis()/refined_soundex()/double_metaphone() return NA for strings with no alphabetic characters at all (e.g. "123", "") — there’s no phonetic code for a string with nothing to encode phonetically. cologne() does the same, counting umlauts and ß as letters it can encode. caverphone() is the exception: it always returns a 10-character code for non-NA input (even "", which codes as "1111111111"), matching its reference implementation’s behaviour.

fas.Date() returns NA for any string that doesn’t match the specified format exactly (wrong length, wrong separator position, non-digit where a digit is expected) or has an out-of-range month/day. Unlike base::as.Date(), it does not attempt multiple formats or partial parsing.

fas.POSIXct() is stricter still: on top of the same exact-shape rule, it validates the whole calendar, so "2023-02-29 00:00:00" is NA even though every field is individually in range. This is deliberate and is the one place the timestamp functions are less permissive than the date functions — see Chapter 9.


soundex(c("Smith", "123", "", NA))

[1] "S530" NA     NA     NA    

fas.Date(c("2024-06-18", "2024/06/18", "2024-13-01"), "iso")  # 2nd: wrong separator, 3rd: month 13

[1] "2024-06-18" NA           NA          

fas.POSIXct(c("2024-06-18 09:15:00", "2023-02-29 00:00:00"))  # 2nd: not a leap year

[1] "2024-06-18 09:15:00 UTC" NA                       



fchartr() silently fell back to base::chartr() — why?
fchartr()’s fast path is a flat 256-entry byte lookup table, which only works correctly when every character in old and new is single-byte (ASCII). If either argument contains a multi-byte UTF-8 character (an accented letter, a curly quote, an emoji), the function detects that via a byte-count vs. char-count comparison and transparently delegates to base::chartr() instead — same result, just without the speedup, and without you needing to know in advance.

fchartr("e", "é", "test")  # "é" is multi-byte — falls back to base::chartr(), still correct

[1] "tést"



fnchar() bytes vs. chars
type = "bytes" counts bytes; type = "chars" counts Unicode codepoints. These differ for any non-ASCII input — get this backwards and a fixed-width field extraction (fsubstr()) on multi-byte data will be off by however many multi-byte characters are in the string.

fnchar("café", type = "bytes")  # 5 — "é" is 2 bytes in UTF-8

[1] 5

fnchar("café", type = "chars") # 4 — 4 visible characters

[1] 4


Similarity bytes vs. Unicode code points
Established edit-distance and Jaro-Winkler functions default to use_bytes = TRUE for compatibility. Set use_bytes = FALSE when one accented character or emoji should count as one comparison symbol. Fuzzy lookup defaults to code points. This does not perform Unicode normalization: precomposed and decomposed spellings can still compare differently.
Bytes-encoded R strings cannot be decoded as Unicode and produce an indexed error in code-point mode; pass use_bytes = TRUE when those bytes are the intended data.

title: 13  Troubleshooting & FAQ
text:
13.3 Threading
Does nthreads affect later calls?
No. Functions that expose nthreads pass it to the native dispatcher as a per-call cap; they do not change RcppParallel’s process-wide options. NULL uses the RcppParallel default for that call, a positive integer limits it to at most that many threads, and nthreads = 1 forces strict serial execution. A later call without nthreads is unaffected.
The dispatcher can use fewer threads than the cap when the input contains too little useful work. String-utility, date, and phonetic functions keep their existing signatures and use the default scheduler for their own calls.
Does nthreads help on a machine with few cores?
Not much below 4 cores, and the package’s own size thresholds (Chapter 9) mean it won’t even try to parallelise small inputs regardless. If you’re running inside a container with a CPU limit lower than parallel::detectCores() reports (common in CI and some cloud environments), set nthreads explicitly to the actual limit — TBB doesn’t know about cgroup CPU quotas and will otherwise oversubscribe.
The supported Windows build always uses TBB. On a diagnostic build forced to RcppParallel’s TinyThread backend, values above one are advisory because that backend ignores the native thread-count argument; the dispatcher coarsens its ranges to limit useful parallel work instead. nthreads = 1 still runs strictly serially on either backend. Set the build variable FAST_STRING_TINYTHREAD=1 only when installing such a diagnostic build.

title: 13  Troubleshooting & FAQ
text:
13.4 Regex behaviour

fsub()/fgsub() with perl = FALSE replaced a different match than base R
Where alternatives can match at the same position, base R’s default (TRE) engine takes the longest match and PCRE2 takes the first alternative that matches: sub("a|ab", "X", "abc") gives "Xc", fsub() gives "Xbc". Whether something matches (fgrepl()) is unaffected. List the longer alternative first ("ab|a") to get the same result from both. Everything else about perl = FALSE follows base R’s rules – see Chapter 9.
Patterns that only PCRE understands (lookarounds, atomic groups, possessive quantifiers, named groups) run with perl = TRUE semantics even when perl = FALSE, still on the fast path. fcount() delegates only an empty pattern to base::gregexpr(), because base R counts those matches in characters.
A warning says “PCRE2 error ‘match limit exceeded’ for element …”
The pattern backtracked too much on that element (see the next question). As in base R, that element counts as not matching – FALSE for fgrepl(), unchanged for fsub()/fgsub(), 0 for fcount() – and the rest of the vector is processed normally.
Catastrophic backtracking — am I safe?
Only partially. The prepared fixed = TRUE path treats the pattern as literal bytes, so regex backtracking cannot occur. PCRE2 (used for general regex) is not immune — it’s still a backtracking engine, in the same risk class as base R’s perl = TRUE. If you’re matching untrusted patterns against untrusted input, that risk exists regardless of which package you use; this package doesn’t add to it, but doesn’t remove it either. Prefer fixed = TRUE whenever the pattern is actually a literal string: it avoids regex backtracking and is also the fastest path in the package.

title: 13  Troubleshooting & FAQ
text:
13.5 Getting help

Found a bug, or a discrepancy between fast.string and base R’s behaviour on some input? Open an issue: https://github.com/KyleHaynes/anthropic_fast/issues.
For the underlying algorithms, Chapter 9 has the full detail behind every function’s behaviour.
For exact argument-by-argument documentation, Chapter 11.

title: 10  Clerical review with rLink_inspect()
text:
10.1 A worked example
Chapter 9 ends with a table of scored pairs and a threshold. For the pairs well above the cut and well below it, that is the whole decision. For the pairs near it, it is not a decision at all — it is a coin toss dressed up as a number, and on a person linkage those pairs are where the married names, the nicknames, the twins and the father-and-son-with-the-same-name live.
rLink_inspect() is the step between scoring pairs and believing the result. It opens the candidates in a browser, lets you move the cut and see what moves with it, lets you accept or reject individual pairs against the evidence, and writes every judgement, with a comment, to an append-only JSON file that somebody else can read back, disagree with, and replay.
That file is the point. An afternoon of expert judgement that exists only in the analyst’s head is not a reproducible linkage; the same afternoon written down against stable pair identifiers is.
Two small files, built so that every row on screen is a case a reviewer would actually recognise: a hospital admissions extract and a cancer registry notification file.

title: 10  Clerical review with rLink_inspect()
text:
HOS-0006 | REG-0006 — JENNIFER TAYLOR against JENNIFER HARRIS. Everything agrees except the surname, which scores 0.556. A married name, and no comparator will ever say so.

HOS-0002 | REG-0002 — ROBERT SMITH against BOB SMITH. The given name scores 0.5 and the pair is a link anyway.

HOS-0011 | REG-0002 — ROBERT SMITH against BOB SMITH again, but the hospital’s other Robert Smith: born five months earlier, in a different suburb, on a different phone. The two name scores are identical to the pair above — 1.000 and 0.500 — so on names alone these two pairs cannot be told apart, and whichever rule accepts one accepts the other.

HOS-0004 | REG-0004 — WILLIAM HENRY WILLIAMS against BILL HENRY WILIAMS: a nickname and a typo at once.

title: 10  Clerical review with rLink_inspect()
text:
10.2 Opening the review

out <- rLink_inspect(
    pairs,
    threshold = c(surname = 0.92, given = 0.80, dob = 0.90, address = 0.80),
    band      = c(0.75, 0.95),
    reasons   = c("married name", "nickname", "transposed date",
                  "same name, different person"),
    decisions = "cancer_registry_review.json"
)






Figure 10.1: The review screen. Scores carry a colour gradient — dark means more like a match — the table is grouped into in scope and out of scope, and the pane on the right is the pair in focus.


Six things on that screen are worth knowing about.
The header counts everything, not what is on screen. 9 of 14 in scope (7 by the cut, 2 forced in, 0 forced out) breaks the total into what the threshold gave and what a person overruled, because those are different kinds of fact and only the second needs defending. 9 clean 1:1 and 0 contested say what the scope does to the records — a record claimed by two links is the failure mode a pair-level precision number hides.
Out of scope rows are dimmed, not hidden. A false negative you cannot see is a false negative you will not find.
The pane on the right is the pair. Compared fields first, each with the value either file held, the score it earned, and what differs between the two values highlighted. In Figure 10.1 the whole of TAYLOR and HARRIS is lit up, because nothing in them matches; on the line below, only the REET of 140 COLLINS STREET is, because the rest survives the abbreviation to 140 COLLINS ST. One dropped letter reads very differently from a different word, and the highlighting is what makes that visible without reading character by character. Then every other carried column, because somebody deciding whether two records are one person reads the address, the phone and the email as well as the fields that happen to have been scored. This is the single reason to pass a generous keep to rLink() when a review is coming.
Below the fields: the other candidates for the same two records. Whether a pair is a link is rarely a question about that pair alone; it is whether it is the best candidate its records have. Each rival is one click away, and where there are none the pane says so — “No other candidate for either record”, which is itself worth knowing, and is what Figure 10.1 reports for this pair. For HOS-0011 | REG-0002 it would instead list HOS-0002 | REG-0002, which is the entire basis for rejecting it.
A judgement beats the threshold, both ways. The cut decides the pairs nobody looks at. Marking a pair a link brings it into scope though its scores failed; marking one not a link takes it out though they passed. That is what a threshold is for — a way of not having to look at a million pairs, not a verdict. In Figure 10.1 the JENNIFER TAYLOR / HARRIS pair carries an orange marker down its left edge and the pane says judged a link, overriding the cut.
The stock reasons are bound to the number keys. 1 files “married name” as the comment on the pair in focus. Over a few thousand verdicts that is the difference between comments that get written and comments that do not.

title: 10  Clerical review with rLink_inspect()
text:
10.3 Choosing the cut
One slider and one numeric box per score, kept in step, so a cut can be dragged or typed exactly. Beyond all and any, a rule can be written out — surname >= 0.9 | (surname >= 0.8 & given >= 0.95) — checked as you type, stored with the threshold, and re-applied by apply_decisions().





Figure 10.2: The threshold sweep, and per-row scope labels with grouping turned off. Each row of the sweep is a cut-off; clicking one moves that score’s cut there.


The Threshold sweep panel answers the question a threshold is actually about. For every candidate cut-off of one score it reports how many pairs survive, how many records each side links, how many links are cleanly one-to-one, and how many records end up contested — claimed by more than one link. You almost never know the truth; you always know when a cut-off starts producing records that two different people claim.
The same evidence is available at the console, which is where it belongs for a scripted run:

threshold_sweep(pairs, "surname")[
    , c("threshold", "n_pairs", "n_one_to_one", "n_conflict_1", "n_conflict_2")]

  threshold n_pairs n_one_to_one n_conflict_1 n_conflict_2
1 1.0000000       9            7            0            1
2 0.9708333      10            8            0            1
3 0.9666667      11            9            0            1
4 0.9571429      12           10            0            1
5 0.9333333      13           11            0            1
6 0.5555556      14           12            0            1


Read the n_conflict_2 column: it is 1 at every cut-off, including the strictest. REG-0002 is claimed by both Robert Smith pairs, and both score a flat 1.000 on surname, so no cut on this score will ever separate them — tightening it only throws away good links while the conflict survives. The sweep says that without being told the answer, and what it is saying is stop moving this slider and go and look.
Suggest a cut reads that sweep and proposes the last cut-off that buys more clean one-to-one links than it does contested records, and says so in a sentence. Clicking a row of the sweep table moves that score’s cut there, so the evidence and the control are the same object.
Which score the sweep is about is chosen in the sidebar. That matters: it is the second and third fields, not the first, where a reviewer has least idea where the cut belongs.

title: 10  Clerical review with rLink_inspect()
text:
10.4 Which pairs to look at
A threshold is a way of not having to look at every pair. Three features are about choosing which ones to look at instead.
The review band is a range of one score — band = c(0.75, 0.95) above, or the two boxes in the sidebar — inside which a cut cannot be trusted and a person has to look. The header counts the pairs in it, how many have been judged and how many are left, which is the review’s progress bar. Show > in the review band, undecided lists what is left. The cut still decides any pair nobody gets to.
The queue is the max_pairs pairs put on screen (20,000 by default), chosen by review_order(). It opens as the pairs nearest the cut — the ones a threshold cannot settle — and Rebuild the queue draws it again around the cut as it now stands, or around the band, or as an audit sample. Pairs already judged stay in it wherever the cut has gone.

# The same ordering at the console: the pairs a cut of 0.92 on the surname
# settles least confidently come first, and the settled ones come last.
pairs$pair_id[review_order(pairs$surname, threshold = 0.92)]

 [1] "HOS-0012|REG-0011" "HOS-0001|REG-0001" "HOS-0010|REG-0010"
 [4] "HOS-0004|REG-0004" "HOS-0002|REG-0002" "HOS-0003|REG-0003"
 [7] "HOS-0005|REG-0005" "HOS-0007|REG-0007" "HOS-0008|REG-0008"
[10] "HOS-0009|REG-0009" "HOS-0011|REG-0002" "HOS-0013|REG-0012"
[13] "HOS-0014|REG-0013" "HOS-0006|REG-0006"


Note where the married-name pair lands: last. It is 0.36 below the cut, so by distance it is the most settled pair in the file — and it is also the one the cut gets most wrong. Distance from a cut is a good way to find the pairs a threshold cannot settle; it is not a way to find the pairs a threshold settles wrongly. That is what the review band and the audit sample are for.
The audit sample answers the other question a linkage is always asked: of the pairs the cut lets through unseen, how many are wrong? It is a fixed sample of them — the ones whose identifiers hash smallest, so it is the same sample whoever opens the review, and drawing it does not disturb the random number stream. Judge it and the header estimates the false-link rate with a 95% interval.
The band and the audit are both filed alongside a recorded threshold, because “0.82” and “0.82, having looked at everything between 0.75 and 0.95 and found three wrong links in a sample of 200” are different claims.

title: 10  Clerical review with rLink_inspect()
text:
10.5 Judging pairs
Three buttons and a comment box on every row, and the same on the pair beside the table. Ctrl-click (cmd-click) marks rows, shift-click marks a range, and the marked set is judged in one action — which is how a block of obvious links is dealt with without 200 clicks. Marks follow the pair, not the row position, so they survive sorting, filtering and paging.
The whole review can be done from the keyboard, which is most of what makes a few thousand verdicts bearable:






Key





j k, or the arrows
the next and the previous pair, turning the page at either end



y n

a link, not a link — then on to the next pair nobody has judged


u
undecided again


x
mark or unmark the pair in focus


c
write a comment (Esc to come back)



1 to 9

file one of the stock reasons as the comment


Ctrl+Z
take the last action back


?
show this list



Taking an action back is itself recorded. The log is append-only, and a verdict reached and then withdrawn is a different history from one never reached. A comment is saved as it is typed, so closing the tab loses nothing.
Because an override is a decision somebody has to defend, it is reported as one rather than folded into the total: the scope cell says forced in or forced out where the judgement contradicts the cut and confirmed where it agrees (both visible in Figure 10.2); those rows carry a marker down their left edge; the header breaks the total into what the cut gave and what was forced either way; and Show > overriding the cut lists exactly that set — which is the page to re-read before a linkage is signed off.

title: 10  Clerical review with rLink_inspect()
text:
10.6 What gets written
Closing with Finish and close returns a read_decisions() object, so out holds the whole review. The same file can be read back at any time by anyone:

# This chapter cannot click anything, so here is the file as it stands the
# moment the review opens: the run recorded, the opening cut recorded, and
# nobody has judged a pair yet. `launch = FALSE` is what makes that
# reproducible -- the file is written either way.
review_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "cancer_registry_review.json")
unlink(c(review_file, paste0(review_file, ".bak")))
invisible(rLink_inspect(
    pairs, decisions = review_file, reviewer = "a.analyst",
    threshold = c(surname = 0.92, given = 0.80, dob = 0.90, address = 0.80),
    band = c(0.75, 0.95), launch = FALSE,
    reasons = c("married name", "nickname", "transposed date",
                "same name, different person")))


held <- read_decisions(review_file)
held

── Pair decisions ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
File: C:/Users/kyleh/AppData/Local/Temp/Rtmpi4YLwo/cancer_registry_review.json
1 session, 0 decision events

Sessions
  reviewer                  started n_pairs n_shown truncated
 a.analyst 2026-11-12T19:19:02.917Z      14      14     FALSE

Thresholds accepted
  2026-11-12T19:19:02.917Z by a.analyst: surname >= 0.92 & given >= 0.8 & dob >= 0.9 & address >= 0.8
      Given to rLink_inspect() when the review was opened.

── Put this in your script ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Re-open this review, decisions and all:
rLink_inspect(pairs, decisions = "C:/Users/kyleh/AppData/Local/Temp/Rtmpi4YLwo/cancer_registry_review.json")

# Apply it, adding `link` and `link_reason` columns:
pairs <- apply_decisions(pairs, "C:/Users/kyleh/AppData/Local/Temp/Rtmpi4YLwo/cancer_registry_review.json")


A read_decisions() object holds four things, and each is there for a different reader:
$runs — one row per review session: who, when, on what data, with which package and R version, and a fingerprint of the pair set and the scores. If the data has moved under a set of decisions, this is what says so.
$thresholds — every cut that was accepted, with the note the reviewer typed, the rule in force, and the effect it had (pairs, clean one-to-one links, contested records on each side). A threshold with a reason attached is an audit trail; a threshold in a script is a magic number.
$decisions — one row per reviewer per pair: the verdict, the comment, and the scores the pair had at the moment it was judged. That last part matters when the comparators are later changed.
$disagreements — where two reviewers judged the same pair differently. This is the whole reason the file is append-only: a second reviewer’s session is added to it, never written over it. Reopening a file restores your own verdicts and comments, and shows another reviewer’s against each pair without filling them in for you — a QA pass that opens pre-answered is not a check.
Printing the object ends with the R needed to reproduce and apply exactly these decisions, ready to paste into the script.
Applying them

decided <- apply_decisions(pairs, review_file)

Nobody judged anything in this file, so every verdict above is the recorded threshold’s — and it is worth reading as an indictment of thresholds. Seven of the fourteen are refused, and six of those seven are true links:







Pair
Refused on
What it really is



HOS-0002 REG-0002

given 0.50

HOS-0003 REG-0003

Every one of the six mistakes has the same shape: a single field disagrees for a reason that is not evidence against identity, and every other field agrees. The one correct refusal is right for a good reason — two other fields, the date of birth and the address, carry evidence the names do not.
And that is the trap. The obvious fix is to loosen the given cut, but HOS-0002 | REG-0002 (a link) and HOS-0011 | REG-0002 (not one) score identically on both name fields — 1.000 and 0.500. No cut on a name score can ever accept the first and refuse the second. Separating them has to come from somewhere else: another field, a weight that combines them (Section 10.8), or a person.
apply_decisions() resolves the threshold and the per-pair judgements in the same order the app displayed them: the recorded threshold decides every pair nobody looked at, and a per-pair verdict overrides it either way. The counts on screen are therefore the counts the next run produces — a reviewer can include a pair the cut threw out and watch the header agree with them.
It adds a link column and a link_reason saying why each pair is or is not a link: the threshold, or a named reviewer’s verdict.

title: 10  Clerical review with rLink_inspect()
section: 10.7 Why pair_id decides whether any of this survives
text:
10.7 Why pair_id decides whether any of this survives
Decisions are filed against pair_id. They find their pairs again after rLink() is re-run with different blocking if and only if pair_id was built from record identifiers rather than row numbers.

# The same two files, blocked completely differently
again <- rLink(hospital, registry,
               block_1 = list(list(soundex(given_name), postcode)),
               compare = list(surname = jaro_winkler(surname),
                              given   = jaro_winkler(given_name)),
               keep = character())
c(first_run = nrow(pairs), second_run = nrow(again),
  shared_ids = length(intersect(pairs$pair_id, again$pair_id)),
  married_name_pair_still_named =
      "HOS-0006|REG-0006" %in% intersect(pairs$pair_id, again$pair_id))

                    first_run                    second_run 
                           14                             8 
                   shared_ids married_name_pair_still_named 
                            8                             1 


The second run finds a different, smaller set of candidates, and the pairs it shares with the first still carry the same names. So the verdict “married name, this is a link”, recorded against HOS-0006|REG-0006, still finds its pair. Row numbers would not have survived: index_1 and index_2 mean whatever the inputs happened to contain that day.
The app says so itself when it cannot promise this: open it on pairs whose pair_id is a sequence number and a banner appears saying the decisions will not find their pairs again. If you intend to review a linkage, give rLink() a pair_id — see Section 9.5.

title: 10  Clerical review with rLink_inspect()
section: 10.8 Weights, and reviewing on one number instead of five
text:
10.8 Weights, and reviewing on one number instead of five
With rLink_weights() the cut is on the match probability alone, the field scores become the evidence behind it, and the pair pane also reports how many bits each field contributed to the weight. For a linkage with six or eight comparators that is a far easier review: one slider, and an explanation per pair of where the number came from.

scored <- rLink_weights(pairs)
head(scored[order(-weight),
            c("pair_id", "surname", "given", "dob", "weight", "probability")],
     5)

             pair_id   surname given   dob   weight probability
              <char>     <num> <num> <num>    <num>       <num>
1: HOS-0006|REG-0006 0.5555556     1   1.0 64.31631           1
2: HOS-0013|REG-0012 1.0000000     1   0.5 63.50895           1
3: HOS-0001|REG-0001 0.9571429     1   1.0 35.26695           1
4: HOS-0010|REG-0010 0.9666667     1   1.0 35.26695           1
5: HOS-0007|REG-0007 1.0000000     1   1.0 33.36006           1


Fourteen pairs is far too few to fit a Fellegi-Sunter model — every probability here comes out at 1, which is what overfitting looks like, and Chapter 9 fits one on 34,000 candidates instead. But the ordering is already saying something true: the married-name pair ranks first. The model has worked out from the data that surname disagreement is common among matches and that agreement on everything else is rare among non-matches, which is precisely the judgement a reviewer makes by hand in Figure 10.1.

rLink_inspect(scored, threshold = c(probability = 0.9),
              band = c(0.2, 0.95))

title: 10  Clerical review with rLink_inspect()
text:
10.9 Running it without a browser
launch defaults to interactive(), so the decisions file is still written — and an unwritable path still fails loudly — when the call is made from a script or a test. With launch = FALSE the shiny.appobj comes back invisibly, to be run or inspected later.

built <- rLink_inspect(pairs, decisions = file.path(tempdir(), "qa.json"),
                       launch = FALSE)
class(built)

[1] "shiny.appobj"

basename(list.files(tempdir(), pattern = "qa.json$", full.names = TRUE))

[1] "qa.json"


The file is written as soon as the app is built, with the opening threshold if one was given, so a bad path is an error now rather than after an hour of review, and the file records that this data was opened even if nothing was decided.

title: 10  Clerical review with rLink_inspect()
text:
10.10 Argument reference






Argument
What it is for



x
Candidate pairs: an rLink() result, or any frame with index_1/index_2 or x_index/y_index.


decisions
Path to the JSON file. Read and appended to when it exists, created when it does not.


reviewer
Who is reviewing. Defaults to the logged-in user; every decision is attributed to it.


scores
Score columns to threshold. NULL reads them from attr(x, "compare").


threshold
Named starting cuts, e.g. c(surname = 0.92). Recorded in the file as an accepted threshold.


band
Review band on the first score: the range a person has to look at.


reasons
Up to nine stock comments, bound to the number keys.


max_pairs
Most rows on screen, 20000 by default. Every count is still computed over all pairs.


page_size
Rows per page, 5 to 1000.


order_by

"review" (nearest the cut first), "score", or "input".


font_size
Base font in pixels, adjustable in the app.


launch
Whether to run the app. Defaults to interactive().



Limits worth knowing
At most max_pairs rows go on screen; the analysis still reads every pair, and the app says so. reactable draws every row of a page, so page_size is capped at 1000 — there is deliberately no “show all rows”, because at these sizes it would lock the browser tab rather than show you anything. The threshold sweep is drawn over at most 200 cut-offs, placed at quantiles of the score once it has more distinct values than that. Columns are reordered and hidden by dragging them between the Shown and Hidden lists in the sidebar, because reactable cannot drag a table header.
The app needs shiny, reactable, jsonlite, bslib and sortable, all of which are Suggests.

title: 9  Linking people with rLink()
text:
9.1 The smallest useful call
Chapter 6 introduces rLink() alongside the rest of the linkage toolbox. This chapter is about rLink() itself, worked from the simplest call that does anything useful up to a staged production linkage, on the one problem the function was written for: deciding which records are the same person.
Person linkage has a shape of its own. The fields are a name — split into first, middle and last in one system and not split at all in the next — a date of birth, an address, a postcode, a phone number, an email address and a sex or gender code. Each of them fails in its own way, and the whole craft of the thing is knowing which failure you are looking at:
The recurring lesson is in the last column. For a near-identifier — phone, email, address — agreement and disagreement are not mirror images, and a missing value is a third thing again, not a disagreement. Most of the advanced material below is about building comparisons that respect that.
Two tiny files: five people in one, and four of the same five, recorded differently, in the other.
hospital <- data.frame(
    frame_id   = c("HOS-01", "HOS-02", "HOS-03", "HOS-04", "HOS-05"),
    first_name = c("MARGARET", "ROBERT", "THI MINH", "WILLIAM", "ELENI"),
    last_name  = c("O'BRIEN", "SMITH", "NGUYEN", "WILLIAMS", "PAPADOPOULOS"),
    dob        = as.Date(c("1948-11-02", "1979-07-23", "1962-03-14",
                           "1990-06-08", "1955-01-30")),
    postcode   = c("3121", "4000", "4032", "3065", "3181")
)
registry <- data.frame(
    frame_id   = c("REG-A", "REG-B", "REG-C", "REG-D"),
    first_name = c("MARGARET", "BOB", "MINH", "BILL"),
    last_name  = c("OBRIEN", "SMITH", "NGUYEN", "WILIAMS"),
    dob        = as.Date(c("1948-11-02", "1979-07-23", "1962-03-14",
                           "1990-06-08")),
    postcode   = c("3121", "4000", "4032", "3065")
)
rLink() needs two things: where to look (block_1) and what to measure (compare).
pairs <- rLink(
    hospital, registry,
    block_1 = list(dob),
    compare = list(last  = jaro_winkler(last_name),
                   first = jaro_winkler(first_name))
)
pairs[, c("pair_id", "last_name_1", "last_name_2",
          "first_name_1", "first_name_2", "last", "first")]

        pair_id last_name_1 last_name_2 first_name_1 first_name_2      last
         <char>      <char>      <char>       <char>       <char>     <num>
1: HOS-01|REG-A     O'BRIEN      OBRIEN     MARGARET     MARGARET 0.9571429
2: HOS-02|REG-B       SMITH       SMITH       ROBERT          BOB 1.0000000
3: HOS-03|REG-C      NGUYEN      NGUYEN     THI MINH         MINH 1.0000000
4: HOS-04|REG-D    WILLIAMS     WILIAMS      WILLIAM         BILL 0.9708333
       first
       <num>
1: 1.0000000
2: 0.5000000
3: 0.4166667
4: 0.7261905
Four things happened that are worth naming, because everything later in this chapter is a variation on them.
block_1 is where to look. Comparing every record with every other record is quadratic and almost all of it is wasted. Blocking on dob says: only ever compare two people born on the same day. That is four comparisons here instead of twenty.
compare is what to measure. Each element is a comparator call whose first argument is the column to compare. The score column is named after the list element — last, first — and an unnamed element falls back to <column>_<comparator>.
Both are ordinary R expressions evaluated against the data. Nothing was prepared beforehand. soundex(last_name) or fsubstr(postcode, 1, 2) would have worked exactly as well as a bare column name, in either argument.
1 always means an exact match. jaro_winkler() already returns 1 for identical strings, but levenshtein() returns 0 and the RapidFuzz fuzz_*() scorers return 100. rLink() probes each comparator and converts, so you never have to remember which way a metric runs:
rLink(hospital, registry, block_1 = list(dob),
      compare = list(lev = levenshtein(last_name)))$lev

[1] 0.8571429 1.0000000 1.0000000 0.8750000
What it decided is recorded on the result, and is worth reading once per project:
attr(pairs, "compare")

  score   comparator   column_1   column_2      scale direction n_scored
1  last jaro_winkler  last_name  last_name similarity    higher        4
2 first jaro_winkler first_name first_name similarity    higher        4

Deduplicating one file
With one data frame and no second, rLink() finds the duplicates inside it: pairs come back with index_1 < index_2, and no record is paired with itself.

intake <- data.frame(
    first_name = c("JENNIFER", "JEN", "DAVID", "DAVE", "PRIYA"),
    last_name  = c("TAYLOR", "TAYLOR", "ANDERSON", "ANDERSEN", "PATEL"),
    dob        = as.Date(c("1971-09-19", "1971-09-19", "1964-02-29",
                           "1964-02-29", "1993-04-27"))
)
rLink(intake, block_1 = list(dob),
      compare = list(last = jaro_winkler(last_name)))[
          , c("index_1", "index_2", "last_name_1", "last_name_2", "last")]

   index_1 index_2 last_name_1 last_name_2  last
     <int>   <int>      <char>      <char> <num>
1:       1       2      TAYLOR      TAYLOR  1.00
2:       3       4    ANDERSON    ANDERSEN  0.95

title: 9  Linking people with rLink()
text:
9.2 Blocking, properly
Blocking decides what the run costs and what it is able to find. A true pair that no pass puts in the same block can never be recovered, no matter how good the comparators are. It is where a linkage usually goes wrong, so rLink() makes it inspectable.
From here on the two files are the full ones from docs/_people.R: an enrolment extract and a claims extract holding the same people, recorded by two systems that agree about nothing except who the people are.

files  <- people_files(n_enrol = 20000, overlap = 0.6)
enrol  <- files$enrol
claims <- files$claims

str(enrol[1:2, ], vec.len = 2)

 $ given_name : chr  "LI" "BARBARA"

 $ surname    : chr  "KING" "WARD"
 $ dob        : Date, format: "1962-12-15" "2014-01-07"
 $ sex        : chr  "F" "F"

 $ state      : chr  "VIC" "VIC"
 $ postcode   : chr  "3115" "3183"
 $ phone      : chr  "0428 262 708" "03 1459 4591"

claims[1:3, ]

  claim_id                patient_name date_of_birth gender
1  C014234 Moore,  Dr Strodull Daclell    04/08/2011 Female
2  C004667          Majan,  Wei Gaboll    30/03/2017   Male
3  C004718       Sanor,  Holor Tekoson    20/09/1977 Female
                    address_line postcode contact_phone           contact_email
1    399 Queen Ln, Footscray VIC     3093               person98084@example.net
2 376 Flinders Ave, Richmond VIC      842  0494 989 121   wei.majan@example.net
3  85 King Street, Brunswick VIC     3193  03 2336 4436                        


The claims file needs standardising before anything can be compared with it — the name is one "SURNAME, Title Given Middle" field, the date of birth is "DD/MM/YYYY" text, the postcode is numeric so 0823 arrived as 823. Chapter 6 does this field by field; here it is in one block.

titles        <- c("MR", "MRS", "MS", "MISS", "DR", "PROF")
street_abbrev <- c("ST", "RD", "AVE", "CT", "PL", "TCE", "PDE", "CRES", "DR", "LN")
street_full   <- c("STREET", "ROAD", "AVENUE", "COURT", "PLACE", "TERRACE",
                   "PARADE", "CRESCENT", "DRIVE", "LANE")

name <- fsquish(fupper(claims$patient_name))
rest <- fsquish(freplace_tokens(ftrimws(fsplit_field(name, ",", 2)),
                                titles, rep("", length(titles))))
addr <- fgsub("^U[0-9]+/", "", fupper(claims$address_line))

claims_std <- data.frame(
    claim_id       = claims$claim_id,
    given_name     = fsplit_field(rest, " ", 1),
    middle_name    = fsplit_field(rest, " ", 2),
    surname        = ftrimws(fsplit_field(name, ",", 1)),
    dob            = fas.Date(claims$date_of_birth, format = "dmy"),
    sex            = c(Male = "M", Female = "F", Unknown = "U")[claims$gender],
    street_address = fsquish(freplace_tokens(ftrimws(fsplit_field(addr, ",", 1)),
                                             street_abbrev, street_full)),
    suburb         = ftrimws(fgsub(" VIC$", "", fsplit_field(addr, ",", 2))),
    postcode       = fpad(as.character(claims$postcode), 4, pad = "0"),
    phone          = claims$contact_phone,
    email          = claims$contact_email,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
claims_std$sex[is.na(claims_std$sex)] <- "U"

enrol$street_address <- fsquish(paste(enrol$number, enrol$street,
                                      enrol$street_type))
head(claims_std, 3)

2  C004667        WEI      GABOLL   MAJAN 2017-03-30   M 376 FLINDERS AVENUE

     suburb postcode        phone                   email
1 FOOTSCRAY     3093              person98084@example.net

Check the blocking before you run it
dry_run = TRUE builds every key, checks every argument, and stops without generating a single pair. On real files this takes about as long as reading them, which means a blocking design can be argued about before anyone waits an hour for it.

plan <- rLink(
    enrol, claims_std,
    block_1 = list(
        surname_dob   = list(soundex(surname), dob),
        surname_year  = list(soundex(surname), format_date(dob, "y")),
        given_dob     = list(soundex(given_name), dob),
        name_postcode = list(soundex(surname), fsubstr(given_name, 1, 1),
                             postcode)
    ),
    dry_run = TRUE
)
plan

Blocking 20,000 x 15,000 records: 300,000,000 possible pairs

(a pair that two passes find is counted in both)

Two columns in that report earn their keep immediately.
n_expected is what each pass would cost. Summed over passes it is an upper bound, because a pair two passes both find is counted twice — but it is the number that tells you whether a design is affordable.
largest names the five keys per pass that generate the most pairs. A placeholder sitting at the top of that table — "UNKNOWN", "0000", a 1 January date — is a key that half the file shares, and it belongs in na_strings or behind a max_block_size, not in a block.

head(plan$largest, 6)

  pass             key n_1 n_2 pairs
1    1 T460|1989-01-23   2   2     4
2    1 S530|1955-11-07   2   2     4
3    1 G532|2001-03-27   2   2     4
4    1 W452|1998-06-18   2   2     4
5    1 C500|1999-08-01   2   2     4
6    2       J520|1957  10  10   100


max_pairs is the same check, made automatically. A run expected to exceed it stops before generating anything, naming the pass and the block responsible:

rLink(enrol, claims_std, block_1 = list(sex), max_pairs = 1e6)

Error:
! The blocking is expected to give up to 128,438,314 candidate pairs, more than `max_pairs` (1,000,000).
  Pass 1: 128,438,314 expected; its largest block, `F`, makes 64,138,426 of them.
Block on more specific keys, add a placeholder to `na_strings`, set `max_block_size`, or raise `max_pairs`. `dry_run = TRUE` returns this as a table.


Several passes, and why
A pair is a candidate if it agrees on the key of any one pass. Each pair is reported once, and pass records the first pass that found it. Inside a pass, list() joins terms into one key, so list(soundex(surname), dob) requires the same surname code and the same date of birth.
That structure is how you cover the error modes one at a time. The design above reads:


surname_dob — the workhorse. Survives spelling, not a wrong date.

surname_year — survives a transposed day and month, which the first pass cannot. This is the expensive one.

given_dob — survives a married surname, where the registered name is gone entirely and no amount of string comparison will find it.

name_postcode — survives a wrong date of birth, as long as they have not moved.

No single key could do any two of those. That is what multiple passes are for, and the whole art is adding the pass that covers an error you can show exists, not the pass that feels thorough.
Because these files come with a known truth, each pass can be audited:

cand <- rLink(
    enrol, claims_std,
    block_1 = list(
        surname_dob   = list(soundex(surname), dob),
        surname_year  = list(soundex(surname), format_date(dob, "y")),
        given_dob     = list(soundex(given_name), dob),
        name_postcode = list(soundex(surname), fsubstr(given_name, 1, 1),
                             postcode)
    ),
    compare = list(
        surname  = jaro_winkler(surname),
        given    = jaro_winkler_tokens(given_name),
        dob      = date_compare(dob),
        address  = jaro_winkler_tokens(street_address),
        postcode = (function(a, b) as.numeric(a == b))(postcode)
    ),
    pair_id = c("enrol_id", "claim_id"),
    keep = c("given_name", "surname", "dob", "sex", "street_address",
             "postcode", "phone", "email")
)

truth <- same_person(files, cand$index_1, cand$index_2)
cbind(candidates = table(pass = cand$pass),
      true_pairs = tapply(truth, cand$pass, sum),
      yield      = round(tapply(truth, cand$pass, mean), 3))

  candidates true_pairs yield
1       9797       9736 0.994
2      22251        590 0.027
3       1354       1206 0.891
4        880        468 0.532

c(true_pairs_in_data = true_pair_count(files),
  found_by_blocking  = sum(truth),
  pairs_compared     = nrow(cand),
  pairs_possible     = as.numeric(nrow(enrol)) * nrow(claims_std))

true_pairs_in_data  found_by_blocking     pairs_compared     pairs_possible 
             12000              12000              34282          300000000 


Read that table as a cost sheet. surname_dob is almost pure signal: it finds nearly every match at a yield around 0.99. surname_year is the opposite — roughly two thirds of all the candidates, at a yield of about 0.03 — because dropping the day and month from the key makes the blocks fifty times bigger. It is still worth having: it is the only pass that survives a transposed date of birth, and the few hundred pairs it alone contributes are exactly the ones the other three cannot reach. But it is the first pass to tighten if the run gets too big, and the one to point at when someone asks where the time went.
Missing keys never pair
A record whose key is missing pairs with nothing. That is what makes it safe to block on an incomplete field: the records with no date of birth simply do not appear in the passes that use it, rather than colliding into one enormous block of NA.
With the default match_missing = FALSE, a missing value in any term makes the whole key for that pass missing. na_strings lists the text that counts as missing — "" by default, which is what makes the blank phone numbers in the claims file behave like absences rather than like a value everybody shares.

a <- data.frame(surname = c("SMITH", NA, "JONES"))
b <- data.frame(surname = c("SMITH", NA))
c(default = nrow(rLink(a, b, block_1 = list(surname))),
  match_missing = nrow(rLink(a, b, block_1 = list(surname),
                             match_missing = TRUE)))

      default match_missing 
            1             2 


match_missing = TRUE treats “missing” as a value in its own right. It is occasionally what you want, and almost never what you want on a near-identifier: two people with no recorded phone number have nothing in common.

block_2, when the files disagree about shape
block_2 gives the second file its own expressions, pass for pass, for when the same information is stored differently:

raw <- claims
raw$dob_text <- raw$date_of_birth               # "DD/MM/YYYY"
raw$surname_raw <- ftrimws(fsplit_field(fsquish(fupper(raw$patient_name)),
                                        ",", 1))

head(rLink(enrol, raw,
           block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), format(dob, "%d/%m/%Y"))),
           block_2 = list(list(soundex(surname_raw), dob_text)),
           compare = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname | surname_raw)),
           keep    = c("surname", "surname_raw"))[, -1], 3)

   index_1 index_2  pass       block_key surname_1 surname_raw_2    sn
     <int>   <int> <int>          <char>    <char>        <char> <num>
1:       3    2946     1 W452|25/12/1965  WILLIAMS      WILLIAMS     1
2:       4    1570     1 S530|28/11/1952     SMITH         SMITH     1
3:       5    9302     1 M312|10/11/1973   MOTIFES       MOTIFES     1


surname | surname_raw is the same idea in compare: the left of the | is evaluated against data_1, the right against data_2. Either side can be any expression, so soundex(family_name) | surname_code works too. Such an element has no single column to name itself after, so it must be given a name.
The sorted neighbourhood, for keys that differ at the end
An exact key cannot put SMITH and SMITHE together. block_method = "sorted_neighbourhood" sorts the distinct keys and pairs records within (window - 1) / 2 places of each other as well as those with equal keys. Methods are set per pass, so a strict pass and a forgiving one run in the same call:

mixed <- rLink(
    enrol, claims_std,
    block_1      = list(strict = list(soundex(surname), dob),
                        near   = surname),
    block_method = c("exact", "sorted_neighbourhood"),
    window       = 3,
    compare      = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname)),
    keep         = character()
)
attr(mixed, "blocking")$passes[, c("label", "method", "n_expected", "n_pairs")]

   label               method n_expected n_pairs
1 strict                exact       9797    9797
2   near sorted_neighbourhood    1573807 1564239


The window also pairs unrelated alphabetical neighbours, by design. It belongs in a pass whose candidates are then scored, never on its own.

title: 9  Linking people with rLink()
text:
9.3 Comparing person fields
Any function of two character vectors is a comparator, so the choice of metric is a one-word edit. What matters is matching the metric to the way the field fails.
Names
A surname is a short string with substitutions and omissions: jaro_winkler() is the standard, and editex() costs phonetic substitutions (PH/F, C/K) less. A given-name field that may hold a middle name, an initial, or the words in another order is a token problem, not an edit-distance one:

a <- c("JOHN PAUL", "MARY JANE", "ROBERT", "LI WEI")
b <- c("PAUL JOHN", "MARY J", "BOB", "WEI LI")
data.frame(a, b,
           jaro_winkler = round(jaro_winkler(a, b), 3),
           tokens       = round(jaro_winkler_tokens(a, b), 3),
           monge_elkan  = round(monge_elkan(a, b), 3))

          a         b jaro_winkler tokens monge_elkan
1 JOHN PAUL PAUL JOHN        0.407  1.000       1.000
2 MARY JANE    MARY J        0.933  0.925       0.887
3    ROBERT       BOB        0.500  0.500       0.500
4    LI WEI    WEI LI        0.667  1.000       1.000


The token comparators win decisively where the words moved (JOHN PAUL/PAUL JOHN, LI WEI/WEI LI), which is the failure plain Jaro-Winkler cannot see at all — 0.407 for two identical names in the other order. Where a word is merely abbreviated (MARY JANE/MARY J) plain Jaro-Winkler does fine, and the tokens buy nothing. Pick the comparator for the error you have.
No string metric recovers ROBERT/BOB: all three score it 0.5, and they are right to — the strings really are that different. Nicknames are a lookup problem, and freplace_tokens() against a nickname table before linking is worth more than any comparator choice.
First / middle / last against given / last. Two systems often split names differently, and the usual mistake is to compare the fields that happen to share a name. Compare the information instead: build one comparable field on each side with |.

# enrol has given / middle / surname; this extract has only given / surname,
# with the middle name folded into the given-name field where it was known.
folded <- claims_std
folded$given_all <- fsquish(paste(folded$given_name,
                                  ifelse(is.na(folded$middle_name), "",
                                         folded$middle_name)))

head(rLink(
    enrol, folded,
    block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), dob)),
    compare = list(
        surname = jaro_winkler(surname),
        # left of `|` is evaluated against enrol, right against folded
        given   = jaro_winkler_tokens(
            fsquish(paste(given_name, ifelse(is.na(middle_name), "",
                                             middle_name))) | given_all)
    ),
    keep = character())[, c("pair_id", "surname", "given")], 4)

   pair_id surname     given
     <int>   <num>     <num>
1:       1       1 1.0000000
2:       2       1 0.9111111
3:       3       1 1.0000000
4:       4       1 0.8909091


Dates of birth
A string comparator is handed text whatever the column holds, which is what makes jaro_winkler(dob) work on a Date at all. But a date is not a string: 1 January and 2 January are one day apart, not two characters apart. date_compare() is handed the column as it is stored:

d1 <- as.Date(c("1985-03-14", "1985-03-14", "1985-03-14", "1985-03-14"))
d2 <- as.Date(c("1985-03-14", "1985-03-15", "1985-04-14", "1986-03-14"))
data.frame(d1, d2,
           string = round(jaro_winkler(as.character(d1), as.character(d2)), 3),
           dates  = round(date_compare(d1, d2), 3))

          d1         d2 string dates
1 1985-03-14 1985-03-14  1.000 1.000
2 1985-03-14 1985-03-15  0.960 0.977
3 1985-03-14 1985-04-14  0.927 0.489
4 1985-03-14 1986-03-14  0.953 0.500


A transposed day and month is a different error again, and it is worth its own flag rather than a tolerance — 14/03 against 03/14 is six months apart, which no distance will forgive:

transposed <- function(a, b) {
    pa <- date_parts(a); pb <- date_parts(b)
    as.numeric(pa$year == pb$year & pa$day == pb$month &
               pa$month == pb$day & pa$day != pa$month)
}
swapped <- rLink(enrol, claims_std,
                 block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), format_date(dob, "y"))),
                 compare = list(dob  = date_compare(dob),
                                swap = transposed(I(dob)),
                                sn   = jaro_winkler(surname)),
                 keep = character())
sum(swapped$swap == 1)

[1] 341


I() is what asks for the column as it is stored rather than as text. numeric_compare() and date_compare() do it for you; a comparator of your own asks for it explicitly.
Near-identifiers: phone, email, address
Here is the point this chapter keeps returning to. For a phone number, agreement is near-proof and disagreement is almost no evidence at all, because people change numbers and households share them. Scoring one with jaro_winkler() is actively harmful: it produces a confident-looking 0.6 for two completely different numbers.
Build the comparison to say the three things that can actually be true — agrees, disagrees, not known — and let the missing value stay missing:

# Compare digits only, so "0412 345 678", "0412345678" and "+61 412 345 678"
# are the same number; NA where either side is blank, which is not the same
# fact as a disagreement.
same_phone <- function(a, b) {
    da <- fgsub("[^0-9]", "", a); db <- fgsub("[^0-9]", "", b)
    da <- fgsub("^61", "0", da);  db <- fgsub("^61", "0", db)
    out <- as.numeric(da == db)
    out[!nzchar(da) | !nzchar(db) | is.na(da) | is.na(db)] <- NA_real_
    out
}
same_email <- function(a, b) {
    la <- flower(ftrimws(a)); lb <- flower(ftrimws(b))
    out <- as.numeric(la == lb)
    out[!nzchar(la) | !nzchar(lb) | is.na(la) | is.na(lb)] <- NA_real_
    out
}

contact <- rLink(
    enrol, claims_std,
    block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), format_date(dob, "y"))),
    compare = list(sn    = jaro_winkler(surname),
                   phone = same_phone(phone),
                   email = same_email(email)),
    keep = character()
)
sapply(contact[, c("phone", "email")],
       function(v) c(agree = sum(v == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
                     disagree = sum(v == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
                     not_known = sum(is.na(v))))

          phone email
agree      6312  7395
disagree  16033 15634
not_known  9703  9019


Most pairs cannot be judged on contact details at all, which is exactly why a missing score must not be collapsed into a zero. The pairs where the phone or the email does agree, though, are as close to certain as this kind of work gets:

truth_c <- same_person(files, contact$index_1, contact$index_2)
round(c(
    phone_agrees = mean(truth_c[which(contact$phone == 1)]),
    email_agrees = mean(truth_c[which(contact$email == 1)]),
    phone_differs = mean(truth_c[which(contact$phone == 0)]),
    overall = mean(truth_c)), 3)

 phone_agrees  email_agrees phone_differs       overall 
        1.000         0.998         0.075         0.322 


A pair whose phone numbers agree is a match essentially always, and one whose emails agree very nearly so — against a base rate of about a third. That is an enormous amount of evidence from a field most people never think to compare, and it costs one exact test.
Be careful reading the other direction, though. Disagreement looks informative here (7.5% against a 32% base rate) partly because this simulator only reassigns a number for one matched person in eight. Real contact data goes stale faster, and real households share landlines, so on a live file the gap between disagrees and not known is narrower than this. The safe design is the one above either way: score agreement, and let non-agreement be NA rather than a confident zero.
An address behaves the same way, with the extra wrinkle that it is multi-word and abbreviated, so it wants a token comparator rather than an exact test. Sex is the cheapest field of all, and it is most useful not as a score but as a condition — see filter, below.
Everything else
numeric_compare() for ages and amounts, compare_levels() to cut a continuous score into agreement levels for a Fellegi-Sunter model, and any function of your own:

enrol_a  <- cbind(enrol, age = as.numeric(Sys.Date() - enrol$dob) / 365.25)
claims_a <- cbind(claims_std,
                  age = as.numeric(Sys.Date() - claims_std$dob) / 365.25)
head(rLink(enrol_a, claims_a,
           block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), postcode)),
           compare = list(age   = numeric_compare(age, scale = 2),
                          years = (function(a, b) abs(a - b))(I(age))),
           keep = character())[, c("age", "years")], 4)

     age    years
   <num>    <num>
1:     0 27.56194
2:     1  0.00000
3:     0 25.12799
4:     1  0.00000


A distance with no upper bound, like years, cannot be put on a 0–1 scale; it is returned as it is and recorded as lower-is-a-match, and every later step reads that off attr(x, "compare").

title: 9  Linking people with rLink()
text:
9.4 Filtering while scoring
Blocking is deliberately generous, so most candidates are not matches and get thrown away the moment they are scored. filter does the throwing away inside rLink():

kept <- rLink(
    enrol, claims_std,
    block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), format_date(dob, "y"))),
    compare = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname),
                   gn = jaro_winkler_tokens(given_name)),
    filter  = sn >= 0.85 & gn >= 0.80 & (sex_1 == sex_2 | sex_1 == "U" | sex_2 == "U"),
    pair_id = c("enrol_id", "claim_id"),
    keep    = c("surname", "given_name", "sex")
)
unlist(attr(kept, "filter")[c("n_candidates", "n_scored", "n_kept")])

n_candidates     n_scored       n_kept 
       32048        32048        10327 


The rule is an ordinary R expression giving TRUE for the pairs to keep. It can name any score, pass, and any column of either input under its suffix. Three properties make it more than a convenience:
Conditions that read no score are applied first. The sex clause above needs no comparator, so it runs before scoring and the comparators never see the pairs it drops. The order you write the conditions in makes no difference; the result is identical to scoring everything and subsetting.
The expensive columns are built only for survivors. pair_id above all — R takes about a second to make a million new strings, whoever asks it to — and then the carried columns.
The 2^31 candidate-pair ceiling goes away. Pairs are generated, scored and thinned a slice at a time, so the full candidate set never exists at once; only the pairs kept have to fit in one table.
A rule that mentions no score needs no compare at all, which makes filter a way to express a candidate condition that no blocking key could:

nrow(rLink(enrol, claims_std,
           block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), fsubstr(given_name, 1, 1))),
           filter  = abs(as.numeric(dob_1 - dob_2)) <= 31,
           keep    = character()))

[1] 9950

title: 9  Linking people with rLink()
section: 9.5 Identifying pairs, so a judgement survives
text:
9.5 Identifying pairs, so a judgement survives
pair_id identifies each pair. By default it is "<id_1>|<id_2>" built from the frame_id column of each input, and it falls back to numbering the pairs when either input has no such column. Two different names are given as pair_id = c("enrol_id", "claim_id").
This matters more than it looks. An identifier built from the records is stable: the same two records give the same pair_id whatever blocking found them. A row number is not.

run_a <- rLink(enrol, claims_std,
               block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), dob)),
               compare = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname)),
               pair_id = c("enrol_id", "claim_id"), keep = character())
run_b <- rLink(enrol, claims_std,
               block_1 = list(list(soundex(given_name), dob)),
               compare = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname)),
               pair_id = c("enrol_id", "claim_id"), keep = character())
c(run_a = nrow(run_a), run_b = nrow(run_b),
  same_pairs = length(intersect(run_a$pair_id, run_b$pair_id)))

     run_a      run_b same_pairs 
      9797      10672       9318 


Every clerical judgement recorded in Chapter 10 is filed against this column, which is the only reason those judgements still apply after the blocking is changed and the linkage re-run. An identifier containing "|" is an error rather than an ambiguous key, and missing or repeated identifiers raise a warning saying how many.
Building it is the slowest thing rLink() does on a large result. filter avoids it for the pairs it drops; pair_id = NULL avoids it altogether, for a run whose pairs will be thresholded and clustered but never reviewed. attr(x, "timings") reports it as its own stage:

title: 9  Linking people with rLink()
text:
9.6 Deciding, and what comes after
rLink() stops at scored pairs. Turning those into links is a separate decision, and the package gives you three ways to make it.
Hand weights
Defensible when the fields are few and the project can justify the numbers:

cand$score <- with(cand,
    (3 * surname + 2 * given + 2 * dob + address + postcode) / 9)
truth <- same_person(files, cand$index_1, cand$index_2)
qs <- c(0.01, 0.05, 0.5, 0.95)
round(rbind(same_person = quantile(cand$score[truth], qs),
            different   = quantile(cand$score[!truth], qs)), 3)

               1%    5%   50%   95%
same_person 0.778 0.786 1.000 1.000
different   0.280 0.364 0.507 0.671


A Fellegi-Sunter model
rLink_weights() estimates how much each field’s agreement is actually worth, by EM, from the candidate pairs themselves — no truth set needed. It replaces the guesswork above with a weight in bits and a probability, and it can adjust for term frequency so that agreeing on a rare surname counts for more than agreeing on SMITH.

scored <- rLink_weights(cand, tf = "surname")
head(scored[order(-weight),

What a cut-off would do, without a truth set
threshold_sweep() reports, for each candidate cut-off, how many pairs survive, how many are cleanly one-to-one, and how many records end up contested — which is the signal you have when nobody knows the answer.

threshold_sweep(scored, "probability",
                thresholds = c(0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999))[
    , c("threshold", "n_pairs", "n_one_to_one", "n_conflict_1", "n_conflict_2")]

One-to-one resolution, and entities
If each person can appear at most once in each file, say so. select_greedy() keeps each record’s best partner and drops the rest, which removes most of the chaining risk before clustering:

links <- scored[scored$probability > 0.9]
best  <- select_greedy(links$index_1, links$index_2, links$weight)
c(accepted = nrow(links), one_to_one = sum(best),
  precision = round(mean(truth[scored$probability > 0.9][best]), 4))

entity <- cluster_pairs(one$index_1, one$index_2 + nrow(enrol),
                        n = nrow(enrol) + nrow(claims_std))

title: 9  Linking people with rLink()
text:
9.7 Staged linkage
A large linkage is rarely one run. The usual shape is a strict pass whose links nobody needs to look at, then a looser pass over what is left, and two arguments keep the second from repeating the first.
exclude names pairs to leave out. They are dropped as soon as they are found, before scoring, so pairs already settled cost nothing the second time. Given as a character vector they are read as pair_ids and found again through the identifier columns — which is what makes them safe to carry between runs, since the files may have been re-ordered, added to or cut down in between.
rLink_unmatched() is the other half: the records that no accepted link reaches, which are the ones a second run is for.

# Stage 1: strict. Same surname code and full date of birth, names close.
stage1 <- rLink(
    enrol, claims_std,
    block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), dob)),
    compare = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname),
                   gn = jaro_winkler_tokens(given_name)),
    filter  = sn >= 0.95 & gn >= 0.90,
    pair_id = c("enrol_id", "claim_id"), keep = character()
)

# Stage 2: looser, over the records stage 1 did not reach, and explicitly
# not re-examining anything stage 1 already settled.
left_1 <- rLink_unmatched(stage1, side = 1, n = nrow(enrol))
left_2 <- rLink_unmatched(stage1, side = 2, n = nrow(claims_std))

stage2 <- rLink(
    enrol[left_1, ], claims_std[left_2, ],
    block_1 = list(list(soundex(given_name), dob),
                   list(soundex(surname), postcode)),
    compare = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname),
                   gn = jaro_winkler_tokens(given_name),
                   ad = jaro_winkler_tokens(street_address)),
    filter  = sn >= 0.80 | ad >= 0.90,
    pair_id = c("enrol_id", "claim_id"), keep = character()
)

c(stage1_links = nrow(stage1),
  enrol_left = length(left_1), claims_left = length(left_2),
  stage2_candidates = nrow(stage2))

     stage1_links        enrol_left       claims_left stage2_candidates 
             9079             10921              5921              3970 



round(c(
    stage1_precision = mean(same_person(files, stage1$index_1, stage1$index_2)),
    stage1_recall    = sum(same_person(files, stage1$index_1,
                                       stage1$index_2)) /
                       true_pair_count(files)), 4)

stage1_precision    stage1_recall 
          1.0000           0.7566 


Stage 1 is perfectly precise on this data, and that is the point: those links never need a human. Stage 2 is where the judgement is, and Chapter 10 is about making that judgement recordable.
One trap in that code. Stage 2 was run on subsets, so its index_1 and index_2 are positions in enrol[left_1, ] and claims_std[left_2, ], not in the original files — left_1[index_1] converts them back. This is precisely why a stable pair_id is worth having: it means the same thing in both stages, so the two results stack without any index arithmetic at all.
The same two arguments also express “re-run with better blocking, but do not ask me about the pairs I have already ruled on”:

again <- rLink(enrol, claims_std,
               block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), postcode)),
               compare = list(sn = jaro_winkler(surname)),
               pair_id = c("enrol_id", "claim_id"),
               exclude = stage1$pair_id,
               keep    = character())
unlist(attr(again, "exclude"))

   n_given  n_unknown n_excluded 
      9079          0       7836

9.8 Candidates from somewhere else
pairs scores candidates found any other way, instead of blocking: any data frame with x_index and y_index, which is the shape minhash_pairs(), fuzzy_within() and tfidf_top_n() all return. It is the escape hatch for when no key is good enough — long free-text addresses, organisation names, anything where the useful signal is spread across the whole string.

near <- tfidf_top_n(claims_std$street_address[1:200],
                    enrol$street_address, top_n = 2)
head(rLink(enrol, claims_std[1:200, ],
           pairs   = data.frame(x_index = near$table_index,
                                y_index = near$query_index),
           compare = list(ad = jaro_winkler_tokens(street_address),
                          sn = jaro_winkler(surname)),
           keep    = "street_address")[, -1], 4)

text:
9.9 At scale
The whole thing on ten times the data, with keep = character() so that nothing but the indices and the scores is carried:

big <- people_files(n_enrol = 200000, overlap = 0.6)
nm <- fsquish(fupper(big$claims$patient_name))
rs <- fsquish(freplace_tokens(ftrimws(fsplit_field(nm, ",", 2)),
                              titles, rep("", length(titles))))
big_std <- data.frame(
    given_name = fsplit_field(rs, " ", 1),
    surname    = ftrimws(fsplit_field(nm, ",", 1)),
    dob        = fas.Date(big$claims$date_of_birth, format = "dmy"),
    postcode   = fpad(as.character(big$claims$postcode), 4, pad = "0"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

system.time(
    out <- rLink(big$enrol, big_std,
        block_1 = list(list(soundex(surname), dob),
                       list(soundex(given_name), dob),
                       list(soundex(surname), fsubstr(given_name, 1, 1),
                            postcode)),
        compare = list(surname = jaro_winkler(surname),
                       given   = jaro_winkler_tokens(given_name),
                       dob     = date_compare(dob)),
        keep = character())
)

   user  system elapsed

  pairs_possible = as.numeric(nrow(big$enrol)) * nrow(big_std),
  pairs_compared = nrow(out),
  blocking_recall = round(sum(same_person(big, out$index_1, out$index_2)) /
                          true_pair_count(big), 4))

title: 9  Linking people with rLink()
text:
9.10 Argument reference






Argument
What it is for




data_1, data_2

The inputs. One alone deduplicates. Never modified.



block_1, block_2

Blocking passes, as R expressions. block_2 for when the files store it differently.


compare
Comparator calls. NULL returns unscored candidates.


pairs
Candidates from elsewhere, instead of block_1.



block_method, window


"exact" or "sorted_neighbourhood", per pass.


max_block_size
Skip blocks bigger than this, with a warning and a per-pass count.



match_missing, na_strings

Whether missing keys pair; what counts as missing.


force_upper_case
Upper-case keys and comparison values. Never changes the columns returned.


normalise
Convert scores so 1 means an exact match.


keep
Columns to carry. NULL is all, character() is none.


pair_id
Identifier column(s) to build pair_id from.


block_key
Add the readable block_key column. FALSE saves one string per pair.



suffixes, score_position

How the output is laid out.


filter
Keep only matching pairs, cheaply, while scoring.


exclude
Pairs to leave out, by pair_id or by row number.



dry_run, max_pairs

Check the blocking without running it; stop a run that is too big.



nthreads, verbose

Thread cap; progress and diagnostics.



And on the result: attr(x, "blocking"), attr(x, "compare"), attr(x, "timings"), attr(x, "filter"), attr(x, "exclude"), attr(x, "n_records") and attr(x, "dedupe"). All of them survive [, order() and head().
